Each cut halves it: 100 g, 50, 25, 12.5, and on. By cut 10 it is smaller than a grain of sand; by cut 50, smaller than a virus; by cut 70, past the DNA coiled inside a cell. You keep halving until the knife cannot divide it and still leave iron.

That last piece is the atom: the smallest piece of an element that is still that element. It takes only about 80 halvings to get there. Cut the atom itself and it stops being iron, breaking into something else. The name comes from the Greek atomos, meaning uncuttable.

Every one of the 118 elements is just a vast crowd of these atoms: gold atoms, oxygen atoms, iron atoms. So what makes an iron atom different from a gold one? To answer that we have to look inside the atom, which turns out not to be uncuttable after all.

Here is the fact every chemistry textbook opens with: the atom is almost entirely empty space. Nearly all its mass huddles in a tiny, dense core at the very centre, the nucleus, while the rest is a near-vacuum the electrons streak through. Blow an atom up to the size of a football stadium and its nucleus would be a single marble on the centre spot, the electrons a faint haze up in the stands. The solid iron in your hand is, up close, almost nothing at all.

boards.title: The three puzzle pieces
layers: That "uncuttable" atom turns out to be cuttable after all. In the early 1900s scientists cracked one open and found it is not a solid dot but a container, holding just three smaller kinds of piece.

Those three pieces are protons, neutrons, and electrons. Here is the twist: an iron atom and a gold atom are built from the exact same three parts. There is no "gold proton" or "iron electron." A proton is a proton, everywhere in the universe.

The protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge) are packed into a tiny, heavy clump at the centre, the nucleus. The electrons (negative charge) are far lighter and swarm the space around it in a cloud. At this level the "type" of matter disappears; there is only counting.

The only thing that makes an atom behave like gold, oxygen, or iron is how many protons it carries. The universe isn't a kitchen with 118 different ingredients; it's a construction set with just three kinds of brick, assembled in different numbers.

That proton count is the atom's identity, and it has a name: the atomic number, Z. 26 protons is iron, 79 is gold, 1 is hydrogen. The periodic table is just the elements lined up by Z, one proton at a time. Change that number and you have changed one element into another, the closest thing nature has to alchemy.

boards.title: Atomic number and mass number
layers: Every atom carries two numbers that pin down its core. The atomic number Z is how many protons it has, which fixes what element it is. The mass number A is protons plus neutrons, which fixes how heavy that particular atom is. Z is the identity; A is the heft.

An atom with Z = 11 is sodium, always. Change the proton count and you change the element: 11 is sodium, 12 is magnesium. The mass number can vary without changing the element: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 23. It is written ²³₁₁Na, mass number on top, atomic number below.

The atomic number Z is the proton count; it names the element, sets its place on the periodic table, and in a neutral atom equals the electron count too. The mass number A is the total of protons and neutrons. So the neutron count is simply A − Z.

Z answers "what is it?", A answers "how heavy is this version?" Together they give the full particle count of any atom: protons = Z, electrons = Z (if neutral), neutrons = A − Z. For ²³₁₁Na: 11 protons, 11 electrons, 12 neutrons. For ³⁵₁₇Cl: 17, 17, 18. Two numbers, and the whole atom is pinned down.

boards.title: Isotopes: same element, different weight
layers: Two atoms of the same element don't have to weigh the same. Carbon comes in at least three versions, chemically identical but different in mass. The only difference is the number of neutrons. These variants are isotopes.

Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; carbon-13 has 6 and 7; carbon-14 has 6 and 8. All three are carbon, because all have 6 protons, so all have 6 electrons arranged the same way, so all form the same bonds. Chemically they are indistinguishable. The only differences are mass, and for carbon-14, a slow instability that makes it decay (the basis of radiocarbon dating).

Isotopes are atoms of one element (same Z, same proton count) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different mass numbers A. They are named by mass number: carbon-12, carbon-13, carbon-14. Most elements occur as a mixture of isotopes, and because chemistry is run by electrons, not neutrons, the isotopes behave alike.

This is why atomic masses on the periodic table are not whole numbers. Chlorine's mass is 35.5 not because any atom has half a neutron, but because natural chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, and 35.5 is the weighted average. The listed mass is a population average, not any single atom's.

Isotopes are quietly useful precisely because they are chemically identical but physically different. Carbon-14's steady decay dates ancient bones and charcoal to within decades. Unstable isotopes injected as tracers light up a PET scan, followed through the body's chemistry as a detector tracks their decay. And nuclear power turns on separating one isotope from another: uranium-235 splits in a chain reaction, uranium-238 mostly doesn't, though they are the same element. Same chemistry, very different physics.

boards.title: Electron shells: where electrons live
layers: Electrons don't orbit the nucleus like planets round a sun; that's a handy picture, not the truth. What is real is that they sit in layers, like the rungs of a ladder. Each layer, each shell, holds only so many electrons before the next begins to fill, and it is the outermost shell that decides almost everything about how an atom behaves.

Sodium has 11 electrons, filling from the inside out: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, 1 left over in the third, written 2,8,1. That lone outer electron is restless, ready to leave. Chlorine has 17: 2,8,7, an outer shell one short of full and desperate to grab one more. That mismatch is why sodium and chlorine react so fiercely: one wants to give, the other to take.

Electron shells (energy levels) are the regions around the nucleus where electrons sit, numbered n = 1, 2, 3 outward. Each has a capacity: shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 up to 18 (but sits comfortably at 8 for the first twenty elements). The outermost occupied shell is the valence shell, and its valence electrons set the atom's chemistry.

This explains the shape of the periodic table. Elements in the same column share the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike: lithium (2,1), sodium (2,8,1), and potassium (2,8,8,1) all have one outer electron, and all are soft, violently reactive metals. The table is not a random grid; it is a map of how shells fill.

One pattern rules it all: atoms behave as if they want a full outer shell, usually 8 electrons. That is the octet rule, the most useful single rule in chemistry. A nearly empty outer shell (sodium's 1) makes an atom eager to dump it; a nearly full one (chlorine's 7) makes it eager to grab. Almost every reaction you will meet is atoms chasing a full outer shell.

boards.title: Ions: atoms that have lost or gained electrons
layers: An atom is electrically neutral, its protons and electrons in balance. Knock an electron off and the balance tips: the atom is left positively charged. Add one and it turns negative. An ion is just an atom carrying that imbalance, and the imbalance changes everything about how it behaves.

Sodium has 11 protons and 11 electrons, neutral. Lose one electron and it becomes Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons, net charge +1. Chlorine (17 and 17) gains one to become Cl⁻: 17 protons, 18 electrons, charge −1. Opposite charges attract, so Na⁺ and Cl⁻ snap together into NaCl, table salt. Neutral sodium metal explodes in water; the sodium ion dissolves in it harmlessly. One electron makes all the difference.

An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, giving it a net charge. Lose electrons and you get a positive ion, a cation (metals tend to: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻). Gain electrons and you get a negative ion, an anion (non-metals tend to: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻). The charge is written as a superscript: Na⁺, Ca²⁺, O²⁻.

Why do atoms bother? To reach a full outer shell. Sodium (2,8,1) sheds its lone outer electron to become Na⁺ (2,8), the configuration of neon. Chlorine (2,8,7) grabs one to become Cl⁻ (2,8,8), the configuration of argon. The pull toward a full shell is the engine of ion formation, and the electrostatic attraction between the ions that result is the basis of ionic bonding, the next big idea.

boards.title: The noble gases: already full, already happy
layers: At the far right of the periodic table sits a column of elements that react with almost nothing. They don't bond, don't burn, don't combine. They are already complete: their outer shells are full, so they have nothing to gain and nothing to give. These are the noble gases.

Helium has 2 electrons, filling its only shell. Neon has 10: 2 then 8, both shells full. Argon has 18: 2,8,8, full again. Each has a complete outer shell, no room and no gaps. A sodium atom is desperate to look like neon, so it sheds an electron; a chlorine atom is desperate to look like argon, so it grabs one. The noble gases are the destination every other atom is trying to reach.

The noble gases (Group 18) are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon, each with a completely filled outer shell. That full shell is exceptionally stable, which makes them chemically inert: they barely form compounds at all. The octet rule, the tendency of atoms to seek 8 outer electrons, is named for this noble-gas stability ("octet" means eight).

This makes the noble gases the key to all bonding. Every bond, ionic, covalent, or metallic, is at heart atoms rearranging electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration. The octet rule (with a few exceptions: hydrogen wants 2, and heavier atoms can hold more) is the most predictive rule in introductory chemistry. The noble gases are the baseline; everything else in chemistry is a departure from it, and a drive to return.

layers.text: - Chemistry studies matter and its changes at the scale of atoms; the microscopic structure controls the visible world. - Element: a substance made of only one kind of atom (about 118 in total). The periodic table is the full inventory, ordered by atomic number. - Atom: the smallest piece of an element that is still that element. It is almost entirely empty space, with a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre. - Subatomic particles: protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral) sit in the nucleus; electrons (negative) occupy a cloud around it. - Atomic number Z = number of protons = the element's identity (and = number of electrons in a neutral atom). - Mass number A = protons + neutrons; number of neutrons = A − Z. Notation: ᴬ_Z X, e.g. ²³₁₁Na. - Isotopes: atoms of the same element (same Z) with different neutron counts (different A). Chemically identical; the periodic table's atomic masses are weighted averages across an element's isotopes. - Electron shells: electrons sit in layers (2, 8, …); the outermost (valence) shell sets an atom's chemistry. Octet rule: atoms behave as if they want a full outer shell, usually 8. - Ions: an atom that has lost electrons (a positive cation) or gained them (a negative anion) to reach a full shell. Opposite charges attract: the basis of ionic bonding. - Noble gases: Group 18, outer shells already full, so chemically inert; the stable state every other atom is chasing.

boards.title: Why atoms bond: the drive to fill the shell
layers: We've seen that every atom is chasing a full outer shell. Bonding is what happens when two atoms meet and help each other get there. Together they reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement than either had alone, and that drop in energy is the whole reason bonds form.

Two hydrogen atoms drift together, each with a single lonely electron, each wanting one more to match helium. So they share: their electron clouds overlap, and each nucleus now feels the pull of both electrons. The two become one molecule, H₂, more stable than two lone atoms, and the leftover energy is released as the bond forms.

Atoms bond to reach a lower-energy, more stable state, almost always a full outer shell. There are three strategies: give and take (ionic, one atom hands electrons to another), share (covalent, atoms pool a pair between them), and a communal pool (metallic, electrons roam across many atoms). Every one is electrostatic at root: positive nuclei pulling on negative electrons, arranged to minimise total energy.

Bonding isn't something atoms "want"; it is a consequence of electrostatics. Whenever the bonded arrangement has lower total energy than the separate atoms, the bond forms on its own, releasing that energy difference, the bond energy. Breaking the bond costs the same energy back. That accounting, energy out when bonds form and energy in to break them, is why burning fuel releases heat and why food powers your body.

boards.title: Ionic bonding: give and take
layers: Sodium gives an electron; chlorine takes it. Now they carry opposite charges, and opposite charges attract, hard. That is ionic bonding in a sentence: one atom transfers an electron to another, the resulting ions cling together electrostatically, and a compound is born.

Hold a lump of sodium, soft and silvery, soft enough to cut with a knife. Drop it into chlorine, a pale green poison gas, and it erupts in a brilliant yellow flame. What is left is a white powder: sodium chloride, table salt. Each sodium gave an electron to a chlorine, and the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions packed into a regular repeating grid, an ionic lattice, every sodium ringed by six chlorides and vice versa. The result, brittle, high-melting and salty, shares almost nothing with either parent.

Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons transfer from a metal (which holds them loosely) to a non-metal (which pulls hard). The product is not separate molecules but an ionic lattice, an extended repeating array of ions. Hence its properties: high melting points (strong forces throughout), brittle (shift the layers and like charges collide), and conducting only when molten or dissolved (the ions must be free to move).

It is far more than table salt. In magnesium oxide, magnesium loses two electrons and oxygen gains two; the double charges pull far harder, so MgO melts at 2,852°C, hot enough to line furnaces. Calcium carbonate is the ionic lattice of limestone, chalk, and seashells. And an ionic formula isn't a molecule count but the simplest whole-number ratio of ions that balances the charge: NaCl is 1:1, CaCl₂ is 1:2. There is no single "molecule" of salt, only the endless lattice.

boards.title: Covalent bonding: sharing is the strategy
layers: What if neither atom will give an electron up? Then they share. Each contributes one electron to a shared pair, and both nuclei are pulled toward that pair, which acts as the glue holding them together. This is covalent bonding, and it holds together almost everything in your body.

Two hydrogen atoms, evenly matched, cannot rip an electron from each other, so they overlap and let their two electrons sit in the space between, pulling both nuclei in: a single bond, H₂. Two fluorine atoms share one pair to complete each other's octet, making F₂. Oxygen atoms share two pairs, a double bond, as O₂. Nitrogen atoms share three pairs, a triple bond, as N₂, one of the strongest bonds in all of nature.

Covalent bonding is the sharing of one or more electron pairs between atoms, usually non-metals. One shared pair is a single bond, two a double bond, three a triple bond, each shorter and stronger than the last. Unlike ionic lattices, covalent atoms form discrete molecules: finite groups with a fixed formula, like H₂O or CO₂.

Covalent bonding is the chemistry of life. Water, carbon dioxide, glucose, DNA, all are covalent molecules. Carbon, with four valence electrons, forms four covalent bonds, letting it build chains, rings, and frameworks of nearly endless variety, which is why it is the backbone of life. And shape matters: the electron pairs around an atom repel into the arrangement that spreads them out, giving water its bend and methane its tetrahedron. In chemistry as in biology, shape decides function.

boards.title: Metallic bonding: a sea of electrons
layers: Metals don't give electrons away and they don't share them in pairs. Each metal atom lets its outer electrons loose into a shared pool, a sea of electrons that flows freely between the fixed positive ions. The ions stay put; the electrons roam. That one picture explains why metals conduct, bend, and shine.

Take a copper wire. The copper ions sit in a regular lattice, but their outer electrons belong to no single atom; they drift through the whole structure. Apply a voltage and that drift becomes an electric current. Hammer the wire and the layers of ions slide past each other while the electron sea flows around them, so the metal bends instead of shattering. Shine light on it and the mobile electrons throw it back, so the surface gleams.

Metallic bonding is the attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons, valence electrons no longer tied to any one atom but free to move through the whole metal. That mobility is the source of nearly every metallic property: electrical conductivity (electrons carry charge), thermal conductivity (electrons carry energy), malleability (layers slide without breaking the bond), and lustre (electrons interact with light).

The bond's strength, set by how many electrons each atom contributes and how big the ions are, runs the whole range. Sodium, with one loose electron per atom, is soft enough to cut and melts at 98°C; tungsten, with many electrons and small ions, is hard enough to machine steel and melts at 3,422°C, which is why it is a light-bulb filament. Alloys tune it further: a little carbon mixed into iron jams the layers so they can't slide freely, turning bendable iron into hard, strong steel.

Step back and the three bond types are one idea in three costumes. Ionic transfers electrons, covalent shares a pair, metallic pools them communally, but all three are just positive nuclei and negative electrons arranging themselves into a lower-energy, fuller-shell state. The only difference is what the electrons do: handed over, shared between two, or set loose among many. That single electrostatic drive builds salt crystals, water molecules, and copper wire alike.

layers.text: - Why atoms bond: to reach a lower-energy, more stable state, almost always a full outer shell. Forming bonds releases energy (bond energy); breaking them costs it back. - Ionic: a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal; the + and − ions attract in a giant lattice. High-melting, brittle, conduct only when molten or dissolved. Formula = simplest ion ratio (NaCl, CaCl₂). - Covalent: two non-metals share electron pairs (single/double/triple), forming discrete molecules (H₂O, CO₂). Carbon's four bonds build the molecules of life; electron-pair repulsion sets molecular shape. - Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, giving conductivity, malleability, and lustre; alloys like steel tune the strength. - Common thread: all three are electrostatic, nuclei and electrons arranging to lower energy and fill shells, differing only in what the electrons do (transferred, shared, or pooled).

boards.title: The chemist's dozen
layers: We count things in groups: a dozen eggs is 12, a century is 100 years. Chemists need to count atoms, but atoms are so small that a dozen of them is uselessly few. So they invented the biggest counting word there is: the mole.
Just as "dozen" always means 12, a mole always means about 6.022 × 10²³ things. It is just a number, nothing mystical, chosen because it is the right size for atoms.

1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). The size is staggering: a mole of marbles would bury the Earth kilometres deep. But because atoms are so tiny, a mole of water molecules fits in about a tablespoon.

The mole is the translator between the invisible and the visible. Because of it, a chemist can put a spoon of powder on an ordinary balance and know exactly how many trillions of atoms are inside, without counting a single one. It turns "weigh it" into "count it," the move that makes all of chemistry's arithmetic possible.

boards.title: The mole in practice: formula to grams and back
layers: The mole is the bridge between the atomic world, which you can't weigh, and the lab bench, which you can. One small equation, n = m/M, ferries you across: grams to moles and back. The periodic table hands you M (the molar mass), the balance gives you m (the mass), and n, the number of moles, is what every chemical equation actually runs on.

How many moles in 80 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? Add the masses: Na 23, O 16, H 1, so M = 40 g/mol. Then n = m/M = 80/40 = 2 moles. Reverse it: you need 0.5 moles of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, with M = 98 g/mol, so m = nM = 0.5 × 98 = 49 g. Weigh out 49 g and you have exactly half a mole. The balance reads grams; the equation reads moles; n = m/M translates between them.

The core equation is n = m/M: moles equal mass in grams over molar mass in g/mol (and the molar mass is just the relative atomic or formula mass read off the periodic table). Two siblings handle other cases: a gas at room conditions has one mole in about 24 dm³, so n = V/24; a solution gives n = cV (concentration times volume). Those three cover most mole arithmetic.

This is the daily arithmetic of chemistry. Every balanced equation is read in moles: "2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O" means two moles of hydrogen react with one of oxygen to give two of water. The coefficients are mole ratios. So the workflow never changes: convert what you have into moles, apply the ratio from the equation, then convert back to whatever unit you need, grams, litres, or particles.

boards.title: Relative atomic mass: why chlorine is 35.5
layers: Look at chlorine on the periodic table: its mass is 35.5, not a whole number. But you cannot have half a proton or half a neutron. The reason reaches back to isotopes: natural chlorine is a mixture, about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, and 35.5 is the weighted average. No single chlorine atom weighs 35.5; it is the average of a handful.

Work it out. Natural chlorine is 75.8% chlorine-35 (mass ≈ 35) and 24.2% chlorine-37 (mass ≈ 37). The weighted average is (0.758 × 35) + (0.242 × 37) = 26.5 + 9.0 = 35.5. Bromine, split almost evenly between bromine-79 and bromine-81, averages out near 79.9. Every mass on the periodic table is this kind of average across an element's natural isotopes.

The relative atomic mass (A_r) of an element is the weighted average mass of its natural isotopes, measured against 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom (which is defined as exactly 12). It is a pure ratio with no units, but numerically equal to the molar mass in g/mol, which is what ties it back to n = m/M. Add up the A_r of every atom in a formula and you get the relative molecular (or formula) mass.

Those decimals are not rounding errors; they are the fingerprint of isotopes, measured precisely by mass spectrometry. The same isotope ratios do detective work: the ¹³C-to-¹²C ratio in a sample can reveal which kind of plant a food or fibre came from, or trace the origin of a drug. The numbers after the decimal point on the periodic table are nuclear physics, quietly recorded in every element.

boards.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
layers: A molecular formula like C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) gives the exact count of each atom in one molecule. An empirical formula like CH₂O gives only the simplest whole-number ratio. They differ by a whole-number multiplier: molecular = empirical × n.

A compound is 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Take 100 g and convert to moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Divide by the smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2, O 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O. If the molar mass turns out to be 180, then 180/30 = 6, and the molecular formula is (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆, glucose.

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the actual count in one molecule. To find it: convert masses (or percentages) to moles, divide by the smallest, clear any fractions to whole numbers, and that is the empirical formula. Divide the real molar mass by the empirical formula mass to get the multiplier for the molecular formula.

This is the detective work of chemistry. Burn an unknown, measure the carbon dioxide and water it gives off, back-calculate the ratios, find the molar mass, and you have identified the compound. For ionic substances there is no molecule, so the empirical formula is the formula (NaCl, CaCl₂): it states the ion ratio, not a molecular unit.

boards.title: Ionic lattices: the giant structure
layers: An ionic bond isn't a lone Na⁺–Cl⁻ pair. It is a giant repeating 3D grid of alternating positive and negative ions, stretching in every direction. A single grain of salt is billions of ions in one continuous crystal, with no separate molecules at all, and that giant structure dictates every property salt has.

Sodium chloride melts at 801°C because every Na⁺ is locked to six Cl⁻ neighbours and vice versa, so melting means breaking all those attractions at once. Magnesium oxide melts even higher, at 2,852°C, because its 2+ and 2− charges pull four times harder. Strike a salt crystal, though, and it shatters: the blow slides one layer until like charges line up, they repel, and the crystal splits clean.

An ionic lattice is a giant, regular, repeating 3D array of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces throughout. From that come its properties: high melting and boiling points (strong forces everywhere), hard but brittle (a small shift brings like charges together), and conduction only when molten or dissolved (the ions must be free to move; in the solid they are locked).

The lattice is why we write NaCl, not a molecule count: the formula is just the simplest ion ratio. It is why salt water conducts but solid salt does not, and why magnesium oxide lines furnaces. The properties live not in any single ion pair but in the cooperative pull of the whole lattice.

boards.title: Covalent networks: diamond and graphite
layers: Some covalent substances are small discrete molecules (H₂O, CO₂). Others are giant covalent networks, every atom bonded to its neighbours in one continuous framework. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet one is the hardest natural substance and the other soft enough to write with. Same atoms; the bonding pattern is everything.

In diamond, each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral network, every electron locked in a bond: the result is the hardest natural material, non-conducting, melting near 3,500°C. In graphite, each carbon bonds to only three, in flat hexagonal sheets, and the spare electron roams free between the sheets. So graphite conducts, and its sheets slide over one another, making it soft and slippery. One element, two patterns, opposite properties.

Giant covalent (network) solids are continuous 3D frameworks of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout, with no discrete molecules: the whole crystal is effectively one molecule. Examples are diamond and graphite (both carbon) and silicon dioxide (sand, quartz). They share very high melting points and hardness, and (graphite aside) do not conduct. Different structural forms of one element, like diamond and graphite, are called allotropes.

This is the sharpest case of structure deciding properties in all of chemistry. Diamond cuts and grinds; graphite lubricates and conducts, which is why it serves as electrodes and pencil "lead." And carbon's flexibility keeps giving: graphene, a single graphite sheet, is the strongest material known, and the football-shaped fullerenes extend one element into a whole materials library.

boards.title: Molecular shapes: VSEPR
layers: Molecules are not flat sketches; they are 3D objects with definite shapes, linear, bent, tetrahedral, pyramidal. And the shape is not arbitrary. It follows one rule: electron pairs repel, so they spread themselves around the central atom as far apart as they can get. That rule is VSEPR, and it predicts the shape of almost any molecule.

Count the regions of electron density around the central atom. Carbon dioxide has two (two double bonds), which push to opposite sides: linear, 180°. Methane has four bonds and no lone pairs: a perfect tetrahedron, 109.5°. Water has four regions too (two bonds, two lone pairs), but the lone pairs press harder, squeezing the H-O-H angle to 104.5° and bending the molecule. Ammonia, with three bonds and one lone pair, is pushed into a trigonal pyramid.

VSEPR (valence-shell electron-pair repulsion) says the electron pairs around a central atom, bonding and lone alike, arrange to minimise repulsion, and that sets the shape. Two regions give linear, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral. Lone pairs bend the shape further: four regions with one lone pair give a pyramid, with two lone pairs give a bent molecule, because lone pairs repel more strongly than bonds.

Shape decides function. Water's bend makes it polar, which makes it an extraordinary solvent; methane's symmetry makes it non-polar, which is why oil and water don't mix. A drug works only if its shape fits its target like a key in a lock, and DNA's double helix is held at specific angles. VSEPR turns a flat formula into the 3D object that does the real work.

boards.title: Polarity: when sharing isn't equal
layers: In a covalent bond electrons are shared, but rarely equally. Oxygen pulls harder than hydrogen, so in an O-H bond the electrons sit closer to oxygen, giving it a slight negative charge (δ−) and leaving hydrogen slightly positive (δ+). That is a polar bond. If the molecule's shape lets those bond polarities add up instead of cancelling, the whole molecule is polar.

The pull is measured by electronegativity, which rises across the periodic table and falls down it; fluorine is the highest at 4.0. Water's O-H bonds are polar, and its bent shape stops them cancelling, so water carries a net polarity. Carbon dioxide's C=O bonds are just as polar, but its straight linear shape points them in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel and CO₂ is non-polar overall. Shape decides whether the bond polarities add or cancel.

Electronegativity is an atom's pull on shared electrons. A bond is polar when the two atoms differ enough in it, the stronger puller taking the δ−. A molecule is polar when it carries a net lopsided charge, a dipole. Crucially, a molecule can have polar bonds yet be non-polar overall if its symmetry cancels them out, as in CO₂ and CCl₄.

Polarity runs by one rule of thumb: like dissolves like. Polar water dissolves polar and ionic things (salt, sugar); non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar things (grease, wax), which is why water alone won't shift oil. Polarity also sets boiling points (polar molecules cling harder) and decides how a drug crosses the non-polar wall of a cell. How lopsided a molecule's electrons are shapes how it meets everything around it.

boards.title: Intermolecular forces
layers: Covalent and ionic bonds hold atoms together inside a molecule. Intermolecular forces hold whole molecules to each other. They are much weaker, but they are why water is liquid at room temperature, why geckos can walk on ceilings, and why DNA's two strands stay zipped. Every molecule feels at least one.

Methane and water have almost the same mass, yet methane boils at −161°C and water at +100°C. The 261°C gap is all intermolecular forces: methane has only weak dispersion forces, while water has hydrogen bonding, the strongest kind. Among the halogens, all non-polar, boiling points still climb from fluorine (a gas) to iodine (a solid), because more electrons make stronger dispersion forces.

There are three intermolecular forces, weakest to strongest: London dispersion forces (fleeting dipoles from shifting electrons, present in everything, stronger the more electrons there are), dipole-dipole forces (between polar molecules), and hydrogen bonding (a strong special case when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine). Each is far weaker than a covalent bond, but they add up: across a huge molecule their total can be enormous.

These forces set the physical properties of nearly everything. A longer hydrocarbon has more electrons, so stronger dispersion forces and a higher boiling point. Water beads on a waxed car because its molecules cling to each other through hydrogen bonds but barely stick to the non-polar wax. And life runs on them: protein folding, DNA base-pairing, and cell membranes are all held by these weak, additive, selective attractions.

layers.text: An atom is the smallest unit of an element. But walk outside and almost nothing you see is single atoms. The air, the water, your skin — all of it is atoms grouped together, stuck by bonds, moving as a unit. Each group is a molecule: the smallest piece of a substance that is still that substance.

Take a glass of water. Divide the water in half, again and again, until you reach a single unit: two hydrogens bonded to one oxygen. That unit, H₂O, is a water molecule. It still tastes like water, freezes like water, boils like water. Split it further — tear the H away from the O — and it is no longer water. The atoms are the same. The substance is gone. The molecule is the identity.

Oxygen gas is O₂ — two oxygen atoms bonded together. A single oxygen atom, O, is violently reactive and does not exist free in nature. O₂ is stable, colourless, the gas you breathe. Same element, same atom — but the grouping changes everything. The molecule, not the atom, is what you actually encounter.

A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds — bonds where atoms share electrons. It is the smallest particle of a covalent substance that has the chemical properties of that substance. A molecule can be an element (O₂, N₂) or a compound (H₂O, CO₂). It has a fixed number and type of atoms — its molecular formula — and a specific 3D shape. That shape comes from its bond angles.

Not everything is molecular. Table salt, NaCl, is ionic — a giant lattice of alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. There is no single "NaCl molecule" sitting alone. Diamond is a giant covalent network — carbon atoms bonded in all directions, one enormous single structure. Helium gas is single atoms. The word "molecule" has a specific meaning: a discrete, countable group of atoms. If you cannot point to one unit and say "that's it," it's probably not a molecule.

A molecular formula lists which atoms and how many. H₂O: two hydrogens, one oxygen. CO₂: one carbon, two oxygens. C₆H₁₂O₆: six carbons, twelve hydrogens, six oxygens — glucose. The formula is the molecule's identity card. Change one number and it's a different substance. H₂O is water. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide — bleaches hair, burns skin. One extra oxygen atom per molecule. The formula is that precise.

A molecule is not a flat drawing on paper. The bonds point in specific directions, at specific angles, in three-dimensional space. Water is bent at 104.5°. CO₂ is a straight line at 180°. Methane is a tetrahedron at 109.5°. The shape determines whether the molecule is polar, how it packs with other molecules, and what it can react with. The formula tells you what's in it; the shape tells you how it behaves.

Every substance fits one of four boxes. Atomic: single atoms (He, Ne, Ar). Molecular: discrete groups of bonded atoms (H₂O, O₂, glucose). Ionic: a lattice of positive and negative ions (NaCl, MgO). Giant covalent: an endless network of covalent bonds (diamond, quartz). The box determines melting point, conductivity, hardness, and solubility. Identifying which box a substance belongs to is the first step in predicting its properties.

boards.title: Bond angles and the shape of a molecule

layers.text: A molecule's shape is not random. It is set by one rule: electron pairs repel, so they push as far apart as they can. The angle between two bonds is the widest spread those electron pairs can achieve. Count the pairs — two, three, or four — and the angle is fixed: 180°, 120°, or 109.5°. Lone pairs squeeze those angles smaller. Add hydrogen bonding between molecules, and the same tetrahedral pattern extends into a 3D network that makes ice float.
Beryllium chloride, BeCl₂. Two chlorine atoms bonded to beryllium — two electron pairs. They repel. They push to opposite sides. The Cl–Be–Cl angle is 180°. The molecule is linear.

Boron trifluoride, BF₃. Three fluorine atoms bonded to boron — three electron pairs. They spread flat in a circle, as far from each other as possible: 120° apart. The molecule is a flat triangle, trigonal planar.

Methane, CH₄. Four hydrogens bonded to carbon — four electron pairs. They cannot all fit flat without crowding; 90° is too close. They pop into three dimensions: a tetrahedron. Every H–C–H angle is 109.5°. That is the widest possible spread for four pairs in 3D space.

Ammonia, NH₃. Four electron pairs around nitrogen: three bonded to hydrogens, one lone pair sitting unused. The lone pair repels more strongly — it sits closer to the nucleus. It squeezes the three bonding pairs together. H–N–H angle: 107°, down from 109.5°. Water, H₂O: four pairs — two bonds, two lone pairs. Double the squeeze. H–O–H angle: 104.5°.

Each water molecule is bent at 104.5°, but the four electron pairs around oxygen still point to tetrahedron corners. Two corners hold hydrogens, two hold lone pairs. In ice, each water uses this tetrahedral template to hydrogen-bond to four neighbours: the hydrogens donate, the lone pairs accept. The result is an open hexagonal cage — the ice lattice — with empty space inside each hexagon. That space is why ice is 9% less dense than liquid water. It floats.

A few degrees of bond angle is the difference between behaviours. Water's 104.5° bend means the O–H bond dipoles don't cancel — water is polar, a powerful solvent. CO₂'s 180° linear shape means the two C=O dipoles point opposite ways and cancel — CO₂ is non-polar despite its polar bonds. Methane's tetrahedral symmetry makes it a compact, slippery ball with almost no intermolecular stickiness — a gas. Shape is destiny.

boards.title: DNA and proteins: the molecules that run life

layers.text: Two molecular structures keep appearing when you study hydrogen bonding. One is DNA — a twisted ladder that stores the instructions for every living thing. The other is proteins — chains that fold into machines. You don't need a biology course to follow a chemistry board. You just need to know what they are, briefly, so the hydrogen bonds make sense.

DNA is a polymer — a long chain of repeating units. Each unit has three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a base (one of four types: A, T, G, or C). The sugar and phosphate link together to form the backbone — like the rail of a ladder. The base sticks out sideways from the sugar, pointing inward. One strand of DNA is just this: a string of bases hanging off a sugar-phosphate rail.

DNA has two strands, not one. They run in opposite directions — antiparallel. And they don't lie flat. They wind around each other into a spiral: the double helix. The sugar-phosphate backbones are on the outside. The bases point inward, toward each other, across the gap between the strands.

A base on one strand pairs with a base on the other strand — that's the rung of the ladder. The pairing is specific: A always pairs with T, G always pairs with C. A and T are held by two hydrogen bonds. G and C are held by three hydrogen bonds. The sequence of bases along one strand determines the sequence on the other — if one strand reads A-T-G-C, the other must read T-A-C-G. This is complementary base pairing, and it is the reason DNA can copy itself.

Because A always pairs with T and G with C, each strand contains all the information needed to rebuild the other. To replicate, enzymes unzip the hydrogen bonds between base pairs. Each separated strand acts as a template — free-floating A, T, G, and C bases pair up with their complements. Two new double helices form, each identical to the original. The hydrogen bonds are the zipper: strong enough to hold the helix together, weak enough to open for copying.

A protein is also a polymer — a chain, but this time of amino acids. There are 20 different amino acids. They are linked by covalent peptide bonds into a long chain called a polypeptide. The sequence of amino acids is the protein's primary structure. But the chain doesn't stay straight — it folds.

The folded chain forms regular patterns held by hydrogen bonds. In an α-helix, the chain coils into a right-handed spiral — like a spiral staircase. A hydrogen bond forms between the C=O group of one amino acid and the N-H group of the amino acid four positions ahead. This repeats every fourth residue, pulling the chain into a tight coil. In a β-sheet, stretches of the chain lie side by side — either parallel or antiparallel — like pleats in a curtain. Hydrogen bonds form between the C=O of one strand and the N-H of the adjacent strand. A single protein may contain several helices and several sheets, packed together.

Hydrogen bonds zip DNA. Hydrogen bonds coil proteins into helices and sheets. Hydrogen bonds hold water in a tetrahedral network that makes ice float. The bond is the same. The context changes. Chemistry and biology are not separate subjects at this scale — they are the same interaction, doing different jobs in different molecules. If you understand the hydrogen bond, you understand the fastener that holds life together.

boards.title: A line
layers: What is a line? A stick dragged through wet sand leaves a straight groove. In general terms, that groove can be called a line.
Railway lines, phone lines, and help lines all use the same word in different ways. Underneath them is the idea of a path from one place to another.
In mathematics, a line is a straight one-dimensional figure with no thickness, extending infinitely in both directions.

boards.title: Infinite
layers: A groove in sand, a railway track, and a laser beam may look like lines, but each one eventually stops somewhere.
A Euclidean line does not stop. It continues without an endpoint in both directions, beyond anything that can be physically drawn.
A true mathematical line is not found as an object in the world. It is an ideal concept: perfectly straight, infinitely long, and useful because of that perfection.

boards.title: Segment, ray, line
layers: A railway track is not a true mathematical line. It is closer to a line segment: a straight piece with a start, an end, and a measurable length.
A ray has one starting point and then continues in one direction without an endpoint. It has a beginning, but no finishing point.
A segment has two endpoints, a ray has one endpoint, and a true line has no endpoints. The difference is the number of ends.

boards.title: The number line
layers: A blank line is not very informative on its own. Once evenly spaced marks are placed on it, the line can begin to carry numbers.
The first important mark is zero. It acts as the anchor point, giving every other number a position relative to the starting place.
Moving right from zero gives 1, 2, 3, and the rest of the counting numbers. Since the line keeps going, the counting can keep going too.

boards.title: The left side
layers: A true line extends in both directions, so the number line cannot stop at zero or only grow to the right.
Numbers to the left of zero are negative numbers. They use the same spacing as positive numbers, but in the opposite direction.
Negative numbers appear whenever a value falls below a chosen zero point: temperatures below freezing, debts below a balance of zero, or positions left of an origin.
Positive whole steps, negative whole steps, and zero form the integers. Integers have no fractional or decimal parts.

boards.title: The spaces between
layers: Whole numbers mark clean steps, but a line is not a row of separated stones. It is continuous, with space between every pair of neighboring integers.
Fractions and decimals describe positions inside those spaces. The point halfway between 0 and 1 is written as 1/2, or 0.5.
The spaces can be divided again and again. However closely the line is examined, more positions still exist between the numbers already marked.

boards.title: Counting on fingers
layers: The oldest use of numbers is counting objects: sheep, stones, fingers, marks, or anything that comes in separate units.
Counting begins at 1 and continues upward: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on. Halves and quarters are not needed when the objects are whole.
This basic counting set has its own name in mathematics. It is called the natural numbers.
On the number line, the natural numbers are the whole steps to the right of zero: 1, 2, 3, 4, and onward.

boards.title: The invention of nothing
layers: Natural numbers work well when objects are present. A separate symbol is needed when the count has nothing in it.
Zero fills that role. It marks the absence of counted objects and also becomes the anchor point of the number line.
Adding zero to the natural numbers creates a larger set: the whole numbers.
Whole numbers are the natural counting numbers together with zero. That is the only difference between the two sets.

boards.title: Walking backwards
layers: The number line includes the right side of zero, but it also continues to the left. That left side is where negative numbers belong.
A balance of 5 dollars is positive. A debt of 3 dollars is negative. The sign records which side of zero the value sits on.
Negative numbers are the same whole steps as positive numbers, placed to the left of zero instead of to the right.
Whole numbers and their negative versions combine to form the integers: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
An integer is a clean whole step on the number line. It may be positive, negative, or zero, but it has no fractional part.

boards.title: Chopping things up
layers: Many real quantities do not land exactly on whole steps. A length, amount, or share can fall between two integers.
Halfway between 0 and 1 is the number 1/2. It names a precise point inside the gap rather than on a whole step.
Any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers belongs to the rational numbers.
The word rational comes from ratio. A rational number is a number that can be expressed as one integer divided by another.

boards.title: Decimals that behave
layers: Rational numbers can be written as fractions, but they can also be written as decimals. The decimal form follows a clear rule.
Some rational decimals stop. For example, 1/2 is exactly 0.5, so the decimal has a final digit.
Other rational decimals repeat forever. For example, 1/3 becomes 0.333333..., with the same digit repeating without end.
A repeating decimal is still rational because it comes from a fraction and follows a predictable pattern.
A decimal is rational if it stops completely or repeats a pattern forever.

boards.title: The rule breakers
layers: Some numbers do not fit the fraction rule. Their decimals continue forever without settling into a repeating pattern.
These decimals do not stop and do not repeat. Their digits keep going without becoming predictable.
Pi is the most famous example. Its decimal begins 3.14159265..., and it cannot be written as a simple fraction of two integers.
Numbers that cannot be written as fractions of integers are called irrational numbers.
Irrational numbers still have exact positions on the number line, even when their decimal addresses are endless.

boards.title: The whole line
layers: The number line can now be built up in layers.
Integers give the clean whole-number steps across the line: negative numbers, zero, and positive numbers.
Rational numbers fill many of the gaps between those steps using fractions and decimals that stop or repeat.
Irrational numbers fill the remaining gaps with decimals that continue forever without repeating.
Together, rational and irrational numbers leave no gaps on the number line.
The complete number line is called the real numbers. Any number with a position on that line is a real number.

boards.title: The name tags
layers: Mathematicians use shorthand letters for common sets of numbers instead of writing their full names every time.
Some of these letters are written in blackboard bold, such as ℕ or ℝ. The double-stroke style marks them as number sets.
The natural numbers are written as ℕ. Whole numbers are often written as W in school-level notation.

boards.title: The foreign letters
layers: Integers are written as ℤ rather than I, because I is already used for other mathematical ideas.
The symbol ℤ comes from the German word Zahlen, meaning numbers. It represents the whole steps: negative, zero, and positive.
The rational numbers are written as ℚ.
The symbol ℚ comes from quotient. A quotient is the result of division, and rational numbers are numbers expressible as one integer divided by another.

boards.title: The big umbrella
layers: Irrational numbers do not have a single common letter as universally familiar as ℕ, ℤ, or ℚ. They are often treated as the non-rational numbers inside the real line.
The largest set in this sequence is the real numbers, written as ℝ. It contains every number with a position on the number line.
The natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, and irrational numbers all sit inside the real numbers.

layers.text: Take a piece of aluminum foil. Cut it in half. Now cut one of those halves in half. Keep going. If you had a microscopic pair of scissors, how far could you go? Is there a smallest piece, or can you just keep dividing that foil forever?

People argued about this for thousands of years. Some said you could keep cutting forever. Others argued that eventually, you would hit a hard limit. They said you would reach a piece of matter so fundamental that it simply could not be cut anymore.
The ancient Greeks called this hypothetical, uncuttable piece atomos.

It turns out, they were right. If you cut that foil enough times, you eventually get down to a single, solitary piece of aluminum. If you force that piece to split one more time, it ceases to be aluminum entirely. You have reached the bottom. That is the atom.

boards.title: Are we sure?
layers: For a long time, the atom was just a very good guess. Nobody had ever seen one, because they are so impossibly small that regular light waves just pass right over them.
So, how do we know they are actually there? Are we certain?
Yes. Today, we don't have to guess. We have electron microscopes that bounce tiny particles off objects to map their surface.

If you put a piece of metal under one of these microscopes, you can look at a screen and actually see the atoms. They look like millions of fuzzy little tennis balls stacked neatly in rows. It is not just a theory anymore. It is a physical fact.

boards.title: The absolute smallest?
layers: If the atom is the bottom of the pile, is it the absolute smallest thing in the universe? Not quite.
An atom actually has pieces. It has a heavy, dense center called the nucleus. And zipping around that center at incredible speeds is a cloud of much, much smaller particles called electrons.
You can smash an atom apart into these smaller pieces. But if you take an aluminum atom and smash it apart, you do not have microscopic aluminum anymore. You just have a pile of generic, raw parts.
An electron from an aluminum atom is exactly the same as an electron from a gold atom. The atom is simply the smallest piece of a substance that still keeps its identity.

boards.title: Elements
layers: So, everything in the physical world is made of atoms. But aluminum behaves very differently from iron, and iron behaves differently from gold. Why?
Because not all atoms are built exactly the same. Some atoms have a heavy center with lots of electrons zipping around it. Some have a light center with only one or two electrons.
These differences completely change how the atom behaves in the real world. In chemistry, a specific type of atom is called an element.
Gold is an element. Iron is an element. If you have a solid bar of pure gold, every single atom inside it is exactly the same.

boards.title: The identity badge
layers: But wait. If all electrons are identical, and all atoms are built from the same raw parts, why is a hydrogen atom a highly explosive gas, while an oxygen atom lets you breathe?
It all comes down to simple counting.
Inside the heavy center of every atom (the nucleus) are tiny particles called protons. The number of protons is the atom's ultimate identity badge.
If you have exactly 1 proton in the center, you are Hydrogen. Period. If you have exactly 8 protons in the center, you are Oxygen.

If you took a Hydrogen atom and somehow jammed a second proton into its center, it wouldn't be Hydrogen anymore. It would instantly become a completely different element. Identity is just a headcount.

boards.title: The inventory
layers: Since there are millions of different textures, gases, and liquids in the world, you might assume there are millions of different elements. But there are not.
In nature, there are only about 100 different elements.

The Periodic Table that you see in science classrooms is not a complex math puzzle. It is simply a list. It is an inventory of every single type of atom that exists, sorted by how many protons they have.
Every physical object you have ever touched or seen is built entirely from that short list of 100 atoms.

boards.title: Flesh and bone
layers: When people hear that the world is built from just 100 atoms, they usually ask: does that include living things? What about a tree? What about blood, skin, or a human brain?
Yes. There is no special 'life' particle in the universe.
A rock is just a massive collection of atoms. And you are just a massive collection of atoms. You are mostly made of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen.

The exact same carbon atoms that make up a lump of coal are currently inside your body, building your cells. The only difference between a rock and a living human is how those atoms are arranged, and how complicated the machinery is.

boards.title: Molecules
layers: If there are only 100 types of atoms, how do we get millions of different substances, like water, plastic, and human skin?
Atoms do not usually sit alone. They bond together. When two or more atoms physically attach to each other, the new group they form is called a molecule.
Take water, for example. You will not find 'water' on the Periodic Table. There is no such thing as a water atom.

Water is a molecule made by attaching two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom. Hydrogen and oxygen are both invisible gases. But the moment they bond together, they form a liquid you can drink. The joined molecule has completely different properties than the bare atoms it is made of.

boards.title: The hookup
layers: So, how do two atoms actually bond? They don't have physical hooks or velcro. How do a hydrogen atom and an oxygen atom hold onto each other?
It all comes down to those tiny electrons zipping around the outside of the atom.
Atoms like to share electrons. When two atoms get close enough, an electron from one atom will start zipping around the other atom too. It flies in a figure-eight, orbiting both of them.
Because they are now sharing a moving part, they are locked together. They are physically tethered to each other by electricity. That shared electron is what chemists call a chemical bond.

boards.title: Rearranging
layers: When atoms share electrons to form molecules, they build the physical world. But these electrical bonds are not permanent.
When a piece of wood burns in a fire, it looks like the wood is vanishing into nothing. It is not.
The heat is simply breaking the electrical grip that holds the wood molecules together. The atoms themselves are not destroyed. They are just let loose.

Once loose, they immediately bond with oxygen in the air, floating away as smoke and invisible gases. The exact same atoms are still there, just holding hands with a different partner. In chemistry, matter is never destroyed. It just rearranges.

boards.title: Mostly nothing
layers: We know the atom has a heavy center (the nucleus) and a cloud of tiny electrons zipping around the outside. But what does that actually look like?

If you look at diagrams in textbooks, they usually show the electrons orbiting right next to the center, like planets huddled around the sun. Those drawings are a lie. They are drawn that way because a true-to-size drawing wouldn't fit on the page.
Let's blow an atom up to the size of a massive football stadium. The heavy nucleus is sitting dead center on the 50-yard line. How big is it? It is the size of a single glass marble.
Where are the electrons? They are the size of gnats, buzzing around in the very highest seats of the upper deck.

What is between the marble on the field and the gnats in the stands? Absolutely nothing. Pure, dead vacuum. An atom is 99.9999% empty space. And since you are made of atoms, you are almost entirely empty space, too.

boards.title: The anchor
layers: We know the atom is mostly empty space. It has a tiny, heavy center called the nucleus, and a cloud of gnats — the electrons — zipping around the outside.
But if the electrons are moving so incredibly fast, what keeps them from just flying away into deep space? Why do they stay trapped in their lanes?
To understand that, we have to zoom in and crack open the heavy little marble sitting dead in the center: the nucleus.
Inside the nucleus, there are larger, heavy particles. The most important one is called the Proton.

boards.title: The invisible tether
layers: Protons and electrons have a very special relationship. They possess a property called electrical charge.
Electrons have a negative charge. Protons have a positive charge. And in the physics of our universe, opposites attract.
If you put a proton and an electron near each other, they pull toward one another like powerful magnets.

That invisible magnetic pull is the only thing keeping the atom together. The positive protons in the center act like an anchor, pulling constantly on the negative electrons to keep them from flying away.

boards.title: The absolute identity
layers: Protons do more than just hold the electrons on a leash. They dictate exactly what the atom is.
The number of protons in the center is the atom's ultimate identity badge.
If an atom has exactly 1 proton in its center, it is Hydrogen. It will always be Hydrogen. If an atom has exactly 8 protons, it is Oxygen. If it has 79 protons, it is Gold.

An atom can lose or trade its outside electrons all day long — that is just chemistry. But if an atom somehow loses a proton, it instantly transforms into a completely different element. Identity is strictly a headcount of protons.

boards.title: The ticking bomb
layers: But if you think about this for a second, there is a massive problem hidden inside the nucleus.
Remember how opposites attract? Well, likes repel. If you take two positive magnets and try to push them together, they violently push back against your hands.
Now think about that Gold atom. It has 79 highly positive protons all crammed perfectly together inside a microscopic space.
The repulsive force between 79 positive charges should be unimaginable. The protons should violently repel each other and instantly blow the nucleus to pieces.
So why doesn't the atom explode? Because the protons are not sitting in the center alone. They have a buffer.

boards.title: The peacekeepers
layers: Sitting right next to the protons in the center are particles called Neutrons.
Neutrons are exactly the same size and weight as protons, but they have absolutely no electrical charge. They are totally neutral. They do not attract, and they do not repel.
They act as physical wedges. They pack themselves between the angry, repelling protons, spacing them out just enough to keep them from blowing apart.
Without neutrons acting as the heavy peacekeepers, every single element in the universe heavier than Hydrogen would instantly destroy itself.
So, the nucleus is a perfectly balanced machine. The protons pull on the outside electrons to hold the atom together, and the neutrons hold the protons together so the center doesn't explode.

boards.title: The hidden weight
layers: We know the identity of an atom is based entirely on how many protons are sitting in its center. 6 protons is always Carbon. 8 protons is always Oxygen.
But protons are not alone in the center of the atom. There is another particle sitting right next to them, called a neutron.
Neutrons have absolutely no electrical charge. They don't affect the electron traffic lanes. They don't change how the atom bonds. Chemically, they do absolutely nothing.
All they do is add dead weight. They just sit in the center and make the atom heavier.

boards.title: The heavy twin
layers: Because neutrons don't change the atom's identity, an element can actually come in a few different weights.
Think of Carbon. Every Carbon atom in the universe has exactly 6 protons. If it didn't, it wouldn't be Carbon.
But some Carbon atoms have 6 neutrons, while others have 7, or even 8.

Because the electron lanes haven't changed, all three versions act exactly the same. They look the same, and they build the exact same things. The only difference is that one is slightly heavier than the other.
In chemistry, these different-weight versions of the exact same atom are called Isotopes. They are just identical twins, where one twin is carrying a heavier backpack.

boards.title: The decimal problem
layers: If you look at a Periodic Table, the weight of each element is listed at the bottom of its box. But the numbers are weird.
For example, Chlorine's weight is listed as 35.5. How is that possible? You can't have half of a neutron. An atom either has a whole neutron, or it doesn't.
The answer is that the number on the table isn't the weight of a single atom. It is a population average.

In nature, about 75% of Chlorine atoms are the lighter isotope, and 25% are the heavier isotope. When you scoop up a handful of Chlorine, you are holding a mix of both. The 35.5 is just the average weight of the whole handful.

boards.title: The tug-of-war
layers: Let's go back to how atoms bond together. Earlier, we saw Sodium throw an extra electron away, and Chlorine catch it. That exchange locked them together to make salt.
But what happens if two atoms meet, and neither one of them wants to give up an electron?

Imagine two Oxygen atoms bumping into each other. They both desperately want to steal an electron to fill their outer lanes. They are equally strong. It is a perfect tug-of-war, and nobody is winning.
So, they compromise. They overlap their outer lanes and agree to share.
Two electrons drop into the space directly between them. Because both atoms are pulling hard on those shared electrons, they are physically glued together. This is called a Covalent bond.

boards.title: The architecture of life
layers: When atoms steal and catch electrons (like salt), they tend to just stack up into rigid, boring crystals.
But when atoms share electrons, they can do incredible things. They can share one pair, two pairs, or even three pairs of electrons at the same time, creating incredibly strong links.
Because they are sharing, they can act like Tinkertoys. They can build long chains, branch out into rings, and fold into massive, complex structures.

This sharing of electrons is the entire basis of biology. Water, DNA, human skin, and tree bark are all built with covalent bonds. Carbon is the ultimate sharing atom, which is exactly why carbon is the backbone of all life.

boards.title: The electron sea
layers: There is one final way that atoms bond, and it only happens with metals like copper, iron, and gold.
Metals don't throw their electrons to a specific partner, and they don't neatly share them in pairs. They do something totally weird.
Imagine a block of solid copper. The heavy centers of the atoms lock themselves into a neat, rigid grid. But they let their outer electrons completely off the leash.

Trillions of loose electrons leave their atoms and just flow around the grid like a giant communal ocean. The grid of heavy atoms stays in place, totally glued together by this swirling sea of negative charge.

boards.title: Why a wire bends
layers: This swirling 'sea of electrons' is the only reason human civilization has electricity and machines.
Think about hitting a salt crystal with a hammer. It shatters instantly. The atoms are locked in a rigid grip, and if you push them, they break.

Now hit a piece of copper wire with a hammer. It doesn't shatter. It bends. It flattens out. Why? Because the atoms aren't rigidly locked to a specific partner. The heavy atoms just slide past each other, and the liquid sea of electrons just flows right around them to keep the bond intact.
If you plug that copper wire into a battery, the entire sea of loose electrons shifts and flows down the wire. That flow of moving electrons is exactly what electricity is.

boards.title: The chemist's dozen
layers: If you want to bake a cake, you need to count your ingredients. You need 2 cups of flour and 3 eggs.
Chemists need to count their ingredients too. To make water, you need exactly 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. But atoms are too small to pick up with tweezers.
If you go to a baker and ask for 12 eggs, you don't say '12 eggs.' You ask for a dozen. 'Dozen' is just a shorthand word for the number 12.
Chemists use a shorthand word too. It is called a Mole.
Instead of meaning 12, a mole means exactly 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000. It is just a massive counting number. Nothing more.

boards.title: A spoonful of water
layers: That number (called Avogadro's number) is so big it is almost impossible to picture.
If you had a mole of regular glass marbles, they would cover the entire surface of the Earth several miles deep.
But atoms are so unimaginably tiny that a mole of water molecules — all 602 sextillion of them — fits perfectly inside a single tablespoon.

Chemists use this massive number because it is the exact amount needed to scale the microscopic world up to the real world. A single atom is invisible. A mole of atoms is something you can actually hold in your hand.

boards.title: Counting by weighing
layers: You still have a problem. Even if you know you need 'a mole' of carbon to run an experiment, you can't sit there and count out a trillion trillion atoms.
So, you cheat. You count them by weighing them.

Think of a jar of pennies. If you know exactly how much one penny weighs, you don't have to count the jar. You just put the whole jar on a scale, do some quick division, and the scale tells you exactly how many pennies are inside.
The Periodic Table does this for you. That decimal number at the bottom of the box? It tells you exactly how many grams one mole of that element weighs.
One mole of Carbon weighs exactly 12 grams. So, if you put 12 grams of carbon on a kitchen scale, you know with absolute certainty that you are holding exactly one mole of atoms.

boards.title: The recipe
layers: This is the daily arithmetic of chemistry. It is how every laboratory on earth functions.
When a chemist looks at a chemical equation, they don't see a terrifying math problem. They just see a cooking recipe.
If the recipe says you need 2 parts Hydrogen and 1 part Oxygen, they don't try to count the invisible atoms.

They look at the Periodic Table, find the weight, and pour the ingredients onto a glass scale. By measuring the grams, they are perfectly counting the invisible atoms. Weight translates the microscopic world into the physical world.

boards.title: Dead weight
layers: We know that protons dictate the atom's identity (6 protons is Carbon), and electrons do all the moving and bonding.
But what about the neutrons? We know they sit in the center and act as peacekeepers so the protons don't repel each other. Do they do anything else?
Chemically, no. Neutrons have no charge. They don't pull on electrons. They don't affect how the atom bonds with other atoms.
All they do is add dead weight. They just sit in the center and make the atom heavier.

boards.title: The heavy twins
layers: Because neutrons don't change the atom's identity or its chemical behavior, an element can actually come in a few different weights.
Think of Carbon. Every Carbon atom in the universe has exactly 6 protons. If it didn't, it wouldn't be Carbon.
But some Carbon atoms have 6 neutrons, while others have 7, or even 8.

Because the electrons haven't changed, all three versions act exactly the same. They look the same, they bond the same, and they build the exact same things. The only difference is that one is slightly heavier than the other.
In chemistry, these different-weight versions of the exact same atom are called Isotopes. They are just identical twins, where one twin is wearing a heavier backpack.

boards.title: The decimal problem
layers: If you look closely at a Periodic Table, the weight of each element is listed at the bottom of its box. But the numbers are weird.
For example, Chlorine's weight is listed as 35.5.
How is that possible? Protons and neutrons are solid physical objects. You cannot have half of a neutron. An atom either has a whole neutron, or it doesn't.
The answer is that the number on the Periodic Table is not the weight of a single atom.

boards.title: The handful
layers: Imagine going to a dog park. Most of the dogs weigh 30 pounds. A few of the dogs weigh 40 pounds. If you average them all out, the 'average dog' weighs 32.5 pounds. There is no actual dog that weighs 32.5 pounds. It is just the average of the whole park.
Atoms work the exact same way. In nature, Chlorine exists as a mix of isotopes.
About 75% of Chlorine atoms in the world are the lighter version, and 25% are the heavier version.
When you scoop up a handful of Chlorine, you are holding a mix of both. The 35.5 on the table is just the weighted average of the whole handful.

boards.title: Counting by weighing
layers: Why do chemists care so much about the exact weight of a handful of atoms? Because it is the only way to do chemistry.
If you want to bake a cake, you count your ingredients. You need exactly 3 eggs.

Chemists need to count ingredients too. To make water, a chemist needs exactly two Hydrogen atoms for every one Oxygen atom. But atoms are invisible. You cannot pick them up with tweezers and count them out.
So, you cheat. You count them by weighing them.

Think of a giant jar of pennies. If you know exactly how much one penny weighs, you don't have to count the jar. You just put the whole jar on a scale. If you know the weight, you know the exact number of pennies inside. That is how all chemistry in the real world is actually done.

layers.text: Three thousand years ago, soldiers stood watch on the Great Wall of China. When they spotted an invading army, they couldn't shout across the mountains. So, they lit a fire.
They burned wet wolf dung to make thick, black smoke. The next watchtower saw it and lit their own fire. Within minutes, a signal jumped from tower to tower, traveling hundreds of miles inland.
To a random traveler, it was just a fire. But the soldiers had agreed in advance what it meant. A column of dirty air became a piece of information.
This is the central rule of all communication: a physical signal can carry a message across space, as long as both sides agree on what it means.
How did this primitive code actually work? It was incredibly simple.
The guard at the second tower only had to ask himself one question: Is there smoke in the sky?
If he looks up and the sky is clear, that means everything is fine. Nothing is happening. If he looks up and sees smoke, that means danger. The enemy is here.
Notice that a clear, empty sky is just as much of a message as the smoke itself. The system relies on exactly two states. Smoke. No smoke. Present. Absent.
By using just two states, they created the simplest possible code. Smoke equals 1. An empty sky equals 0.
At the lowest level, a computer does not begin with words, pictures, or apps. It begins with a very small question.
Is electricity flowing through this tiny part of the circuit, or is it not?
If the path is open and no current flows, the computer treats that as 0. If the path is closed and current can flow, it treats that as 1.
That single choice, between off and on, is called a bit.
Every message, image, video, website, and program is built from these bits. Modern computing starts with billions of tiny switches being turned off and on at incredible speed.

boards.title: The Math of Yes and No

layers.text: People often say computers run on 0s and 1s, which can make it sound as if the machine is doing advanced mathematics from the very beginning.
But at the bottom level, 0 and 1 are not really numbers in the usual sense. They are states.
1 means yes, true, or on. 0 means no, false, or off.
In the 1800s, long before electronic computers existed, George Boole showed that reasoning could be handled through simple true-or-false statements.
His system, now called Boolean logic, uses rules such as AND, OR, and NOT to combine simple yes-or-no answers into more complex decisions.
A computer turns Boolean logic into something physical by building circuits that follow those rules.
Imagine a wire carrying electricity to a lightbulb. Now place two switches on that same wire, one after the other.
For the bulb to turn on, electricity must pass through both switches.
If the first switch is closed and the second switch is closed, the path is complete. The bulb lights up.
If either switch is open, the path is broken. The bulb stays dark.
That is an AND gate. It only gives a yes answer when both inputs are yes.
An OR gate uses a different arrangement.
Instead of placing two switches on one straight path, split the wire into two separate paths that meet again before the lightbulb.
Put one switch on the top path and one switch on the bottom path.
Now electricity only needs one open route. If the top switch is closed, the bulb turns on. If the bottom switch is closed, the bulb also turns on.
The bulb stays dark only when both switches are open.
That is an OR gate. It gives a yes answer when at least one input is yes.
Electricity is hard to see, so it can help to borrow a simpler picture: water moving through pipes.
The comparison is not perfect, but it is useful. A wire can be imagined as a pipe, a switch as a valve, and a lightbulb as the place where flow produces a visible result.
A valve has two basic states. Open means water can flow. Closed means water stops.
That gives us the same basic pattern as a bit: flow or no flow, yes or no, 1 or 0.
The water model makes the AND rule easy to picture.
Start with one pipe leading to a faucet. Place two valves on the pipe, one after the other.
Water can reach the faucet only if both valves are open.
If the first valve is open but the second is closed, the water still stops. If the second valve is open but the first is closed, the water never reaches it.
Both valves must say yes before the faucet can run. That is the physical idea behind an AND gate.
The OR rule looks different because the pipe is arranged differently.
Split the main pipe into two branches, then join the branches again before the faucet.
Put one valve on each branch.
If either valve is open, water has a route to the faucet.
The faucet stays dry only when both valves are closed.
By changing the arrangement of the paths, we change the rule the system follows. That is the basic idea of a logic gate: a simple physical structure that produces a simple logical result.

boards.title: A world without rulers
layers: Imagine you wake up on a planet where measurement does not exist. There are no rulers, no scales, and no clocks.

Someone hands you a rock. How heavy is it? You can feel the weight in your hand, but you have no way to describe it. You can't say it weighs 5 pounds, because 'pounds' don't exist. 'It's heavy' is just an opinion.

How wide is the room? How long until sunrise? Without a way to measure, you cannot describe the physical world accurately to yourself, and you certainly cannot explain it to anyone else. Without measurement, physics cannot exist.

boards.title: The agreement
layers: So, you invent a system. You pick up a specific stick off the ground.
You hold it up and declare: From now on, this stick is the standard. We will compare everything else in the world to this exact stick.
Now you can actually communicate. This table is 4 sticks long. The river is 50 sticks across.

It doesn't matter that the stick is just a random, arbitrary piece of wood you found in the dirt. What matters is that everyone agreed to use it as the reference point. That simple agreement is the invention of a 'unit.'

boards.title: Different tools
layers: The stick works perfectly for distance. But if you want to know how heavy a bucket of water is, or how long it takes for the sun to go down, a stick is completely useless.
You cannot measure a heartbeat with a ruler. Length is fundamentally different from weight, and weight is fundamentally different from time.
To describe the whole world, you need different standards for different properties. You need a standard rock for weight, and a standard dripping bucket for time.

boards.title: The seven stones
layers: Over thousands of years, every civilization created their own random sticks and rocks. It was chaotic. Eventually, the global scientific community got together and cleaned it up.
They stripped away all the clutter and agreed on exactly seven fundamental standards. The seven base quantities.
We have a standard unit for length (the meter). A standard unit for mass (the kilogram). A standard unit for time (the second). There are four others for things like temperature and electric current.
That is it. Just seven core measuring tools.

boards.title: Mixing the ingredients
layers: Wait, if there are only seven core tools, what about speed? Speed is a physical measurement, but it isn't one of the core seven.
That is because speed doesn't need its own independent standard. Speed is just a combination of two things we already have: distance and time.
When you drive a car, your speed is measured in miles per hour (or meters per second). That is literally just a Length unit divided by a Time unit.

Speed, volume, density, force, energy — none of these require a brand new measuring tool. They are all just the 7 base units multiplied or divided together. They are the seven basic building blocks snapped together, describing every single physical event in the universe.

boards.title: The revolution of measurement
layers: Before the 1790s, measurement was a disaster. In France alone, there were over 250,000 different local units of weight and length. A foot in Paris was a completely different length than a foot in Marseille. Merchants used this chaos to cheat people constantly.
