layers: The CPU and the RAM are separate physical chips on the motherboard. To function, they must communicate continuously.
They are connected by the System Bus — a dense cluster of parallel, microscopic copper traces woven directly into the circuit board.
The Bus is split into strict lanes. The Address Bus sends the specific coordinate location from the CPU to the RAM. The Data Bus carries the actual payload of 1s and 0s back and forth.
The width of this highway dictates the absolute capability of the machine. A '64-bit processor' means the Data Bus is exactly 64 copper lanes wide.
It can push exactly 64 bits of data across the motherboard simultaneously in a single microscopic pulse. A wider bus means exponentially more data can move per cycle.

boards.title: The Heartbeat (The Clock)
layers: With billions of bits flying across the System Bus, the hardware requires perfect synchronization to prevent data collisions.
Inside the motherboard sits a tiny quartz crystal. When subjected to a small electrical current, the quartz vibrates at a mathematically flawless frequency.
This vibration drives the System Clock. Every single pulse of the clock triggers one step of the processor.
The machine operates in a rigid, repeating three-step loop: Fetch the instruction from RAM, Decode the instruction in the Control Unit, and Execute the math in the ALU.

This Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle is the absolute baseline of all computing. When a processor is rated at 3 Gigahertz (3 GHz), it means the quartz crystal pulses exactly three billion times per second. The CPU fetches, decodes, and executes three billion microscopic instructions every single second, with flawless mechanical precision.

boards.title: The Von Neumann Bottleneck
layers: The CPU operates at a blistering speed, driven by a 3 GHz clock. It can execute three billion instructions per second.
However, the RAM cannot move fast enough to feed it.

Even though electricity travels near the speed of light, the physical distance across the motherboard (the System Bus) introduces microscopic delays. Furthermore, the capacitors in the RAM take a fraction of a second to stabilize before they can be read.

This creates the Von Neumann Bottleneck. The ALU finishes a calculation in one nanosecond, but has to sit completely idle for dozens of clock cycles, wasting massive amounts of time waiting for the next instruction to arrive across the copper highway.
In computer architecture, a processor is only as fast as the data that can reach it. If the CPU is starved for data, the high clock speed is entirely useless.

boards.title: The Cache Hierarchy
layers: To solve this starvation problem, engineers built a secondary memory system directly into the silicon of the CPU itself.

This is called Cache Memory. It is built using a different, highly expensive physical structure called SRAM (Static RAM). Unlike standard RAM, SRAM does not need to constantly refresh its capacitors, making it exponentially faster.
Cache acts as a high-speed staging area. It is broken into strict levels (L1, L2, L3).

The L1 Cache sits millimeters away from the ALU. It is incredibly small (often just kilobytes of data) but runs at the exact speed of the processor. The L3 Cache is larger, holding a few megabytes, but sits slightly further away.

The system uses statistical algorithms to predict exactly which data the CPU will need next. It pre-fetches that data from the slow RAM and stages it in the L1 Cache. When the CPU asks for a number, the data is already sitting next to the gates, completely bypassing the bottleneck.

boards.title: The Assembly Line (Pipelining)
layers: Fixing the memory bottleneck keeps the CPU fed, but engineers found a way to manipulate the Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle itself to increase throughput.

In a basic processor, an instruction is Fetched. Then the clock ticks, and it is Decoded. The clock ticks again, and it is Executed. While the ALU is executing the math, the Fetch circuits are sitting completely idle, doing nothing.
To eliminate this wasted downtime, modern processors use Instruction Pipelining.

Pipelining treats the CPU like a factory assembly line. While the ALU is executing Instruction 1, the Control Unit is simultaneously decoding Instruction 2, and the memory bus is simultaneously fetching Instruction 3.

Multiple instructions are processed in parallel, staggering across the different substructures. While a single instruction still takes three clock cycles to finish, the pipeline spits out one completed calculation on every single tick of the clock.

boards.title: The Branch Prediction Guess
layers: Pipelining works flawlessly if the software is a simple, straight list of instructions. But software constantly uses 'If/Then' conditional branches.

If a processor encounters an 'If/Then' statement, the pipeline physically breaks. The CPU does not know which path the software will take until the math is executed. It cannot fetch the next instruction because it does not know which instruction to fetch.
To prevent the pipeline from stalling and emptying out, the CPU relies on a hardware mechanism called a Branch Predictor.

The processor literally guesses which path the software will take based on historical data. It assumes a path, fetches the data, and begins executing the math before the 'If/Then' statement is actually resolved.

This is called Speculative Execution. If the processor guessed correctly, the pipeline never stalls. If it guessed wrong, it flushes the incorrect math out of its registers and starts over. Modern predictors boast over a 95% accuracy rate, saving billions of wasted clock cycles.

boards.title: Scaling Sideways (Multi-Core)
layers: For decades, processor speed was increased by simply driving the quartz clock faster. A 1 GHz chip was replaced by a 2 GHz chip, then a 3 GHz chip.

Eventually, this strategy hit a hard wall of physics. Pushing billions of electrical pulses through microscopic silicon generates extreme heat. Pushing a clock to 5 GHz generates so much thermal energy the silicon literally melts.
Because engineers could no longer scale the clock speed vertically, they decided to scale the architecture horizontally.
Instead of building one massive, impossibly fast processor, they took the complete architecture (Control Unit, ALU, L1 Cache) and stamped a perfect copy of it onto the exact same piece of silicon.

This is a Multi-Core Processor. A 'Quad-Core' chip is simply four complete, independent CPUs sitting side-by-side on one square of metal. They divide the workload, executing four separate pipelines of software simultaneously, drastically increasing computational power without melting the machine.

boards.title: A line has a constant change

tags.concept: A line has a constant change
tags.subject: maths

layers: On a coordinate grid, a straight line is a set of points connected by one steady relationship between x and y.
The important feature is consistency. Each equal step in x produces the same change in y.
That steady change is what separates a straight line from a curve, where the rate of change may vary from point to point.
Lines and gradients begin with this fact: a straight line changes at a constant rate.

boards.title: Gradient measures steepness
layers: Gradient measures how steeply a line rises or falls as it moves across the grid.
It compares vertical change with horizontal change: how much y changes for a chosen change in x.
The common formula is gradient = rise / run, or m = Δy / Δx.
A larger gradient means the line changes more sharply. A smaller gradient means the line changes more gently.
Gradient turns the visual idea of steepness into a number that can be calculated.

boards.title: Reading rise and run
layers: To find a gradient, choose two points on the line and compare their coordinates.
The rise is the vertical change between the points. The run is the horizontal change between the same two points.
For points (1, 2) and (4, 8), the rise is 6 and the run is 3.
The gradient is 6 / 3 = 2, so the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit across.
On a straight line, any two points give the same gradient because the rate of change is constant.

boards.title: Positive and negative gradients
layers: The sign of the gradient gives the line's direction.
A positive gradient means the line rises from left to right.
A negative gradient means the line falls from left to right.
A gradient of 2 rises 2 units for every 1 unit across. A gradient of -2 falls 2 units for every 1 unit across.
The size of the gradient gives steepness, while the sign gives direction.

boards.title: Zero and undefined gradient
layers: A horizontal line has no vertical change as x changes.
Since the rise is zero, every horizontal line has gradient 0.
A vertical line has no horizontal change as y changes.
Since the run is zero, the gradient calculation would require division by zero.
For that reason, a vertical line has undefined gradient rather than gradient 0.

boards.title: The y-intercept anchors the line
layers: Gradient gives steepness and direction, but it does not fix the line's exact position.
Many lines can share the same gradient while crossing the grid at different heights.
The y-intercept is the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
At the y-axis, x = 0. The y-intercept is therefore the value of y when x is 0.
The intercept anchors the line vertically while the gradient controls its tilt.

boards.title: The equation y = mx + c
layers: The equation y = mx + c stores the two key features of a non-vertical straight line.
The m gives the gradient: the rate at which y changes as x changes.
The c gives the y-intercept: the height where the line crosses the y-axis.
In y = 2x + 3, the gradient is 2 and the y-intercept is 3.
Changing m changes the tilt. Changing c shifts the line up or down without changing its tilt.

boards.title: Lines with the same gradient
layers: Lines with the same gradient rise or fall at the same rate.
If their intercepts are different, they sit at different heights but keep the same direction.
Such lines are parallel because the gap between them never closes.
The equations y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x - 4 are parallel because both have gradient 2.
Matching gradients are enough to prove that two non-identical straight lines are parallel.

boards.title: Finding a line from two points

tags.concept: Finding a line from two points
tags.subject: maths

layers: Two points are enough to determine one straight line.
First, use the two points to calculate the gradient with m = Δy / Δx.
Then substitute one point into y = mx + c to find the intercept.
Once m and c are known, the equation describes the whole line.
This converts a pair of plotted points into an algebraic rule.

boards.title: Why gradients matter
layers: Gradient is not only a property of drawn lines. It is a way to describe constant change.
Speed is change in position over time. Gradient is change in y over change in x.
This is why distance-time graphs, cost graphs, growth graphs, and many scientific graphs use gradients.
A straight line means the rate stays constant. A steeper line means the rate is larger.
Lines and gradients prepare the ground for rates, motion graphs, and eventually calculus.

layers.text: A single logic gate can only answer a very small question.
An AND gate asks, "Are both inputs yes?" An OR gate asks, "Is at least one input yes?"
By itself, that does not seem like much. But computers become powerful by connecting many simple parts together.
A group of gates can compare two values, add numbers, check whether something is true, or decide which instruction should happen next.
This is the first big idea in system design: complex systems are usually built from simple parts arranged carefully.
Almost every computer system follows a basic pattern: input, processing, output.
The input is what the system receives. It might be a button press, a message, a search query, a payment, or a sensor reading.
Processing is what the system does with that input. It checks rules, transforms data, makes decisions, or asks another part of the system for help.
The output is what the system sends back. It might show a result, save a record, send a notification, or trigger another action.
System design begins by asking three simple questions: What comes in? What happens to it? What must come out?
A system is easier to understand when we break it into parts called components.
A component is a piece of the system with a specific job.
In a messaging app, one component might handle login, another might store messages, another might deliver notifications, and another might show the chat screen.

Each component hides some complexity from the rest of the system. The notification component does not need to know how passwords work. The login component does not need to know how message bubbles are drawn on screen.
Good system design gives each part a clear responsibility, so the whole system is easier to build, change, and repair.
Components need a way to talk to each other.
The agreed way one component communicates with another is called an interface.
An interface says, "If you give me this kind of input, I will give you this kind of output."
For example, a weather app might ask a weather service for the forecast in London. The app sends a location. The service sends back temperature, wind, rain, and time.
The app does not need to know how the weather service gathers its data. It only needs the interface to be stable and clear.
Interfaces let large systems grow because each part can rely on the promises made by the other parts.
Some information disappears after it is used. Other information has to be remembered.
The information a system remembers at a particular moment is called its state.
If you are logged into an app, your login status is part of the system's state. If items are sitting in your shopping cart, the cart is state. If a message has been read or unread, that is state too.
State matters because the same input can mean different things depending on what the system remembers.
Pressing "Buy" means one thing if your cart is full, another thing if your cart is empty, and another thing if your payment has already gone through.
A system designer has to decide what should be remembered, where it should be stored, and when it should change.
Memory inside a running computer is temporary. If the program stops, that memory can disappear.
Many systems need information to survive after the program closes, the phone restarts, or the server crashes.
A database is where a system stores information it needs to keep.
A banking app stores balances and transactions. A social app stores profiles, posts, and comments. A school system stores students, courses, and grades.
The database becomes the system's long-term memory.
System design asks what data must be stored, how it should be organized, who is allowed to change it, and how quickly it must be found again.
Many modern systems are split between a client and a server.
The client is the part close to the user. It might be a phone app, a web browser, or a desktop program.
The server is the part that runs somewhere else. It receives requests, performs work, talks to databases, and sends back responses.
When you open a shopping app and search for headphones, your phone sends a request to a server.
The server looks up matching products, applies rules, and sends back a response that your phone can display.
This request-response pattern is one of the basic shapes of system design.
A system can be correct and still feel bad to use if it is too slow.
Latency is the delay between asking for something and getting the answer back.
If you tap a button and the screen changes instantly, latency feels low. If you wait several seconds, latency feels high.
Latency can come from many places: slow code, a busy database, a weak network connection, or a server that is too far away.
System designers pay attention to latency because users experience delay directly.
A good system does not only ask, "Does it work?" It also asks, "Does it respond quickly enough?"
A system that works for ten people may fail when ten million people use it.
Capacity means how much work a system can handle.
A small cafe can serve a few customers at once. If a crowd arrives, the same kitchen, staff, and tables may no longer be enough.
Software systems have the same problem. More users mean more requests, more data, more storage, and more pressure on every component.
Scaling a system means changing it so it can handle more work without breaking or becoming painfully slow.
System design asks where the pressure will appear first and what can be changed before that part fails.
In any system, the slowest or most overloaded part can limit everything else.
That limiting part is called a bottleneck.
Imagine a wide road that suddenly narrows to one lane. It does not matter how wide the road is before that point. Traffic still slows where the road becomes narrow.
In software, the bottleneck might be a database, a network connection, a file upload service, or a single server doing too much work.
Finding bottlenecks is one of the most practical parts of system design.
Once you know which part is limiting the system, you can decide whether to speed it up, split the work, cache results, or redesign the flow.
Some answers are expensive to produce again and again.
A cache stores a recently used or commonly needed answer in a faster place.
If many people ask for the same weather forecast, the system does not always need to calculate or fetch it from the original source every time.
It can keep a copy for a short period and reuse it.
Caching can make a system much faster, but it introduces a new question: how old is the saved answer allowed to be?
Good system design balances speed with freshness.
Real systems fail.
Servers crash. Networks drop. Databases get busy. A service that worked a moment ago may stop responding.
Reliability is the ability of a system to keep working, or recover well, when something goes wrong.
A reliable system does not assume every part will be perfect all the time.
It might retry a failed request, keep backup copies of data, route traffic to another server, or show a useful message instead of silently breaking.
System design is partly the art of asking, "What happens when this part fails?"
There is rarely one perfect design.
A system that is very fast may use more memory. A system that stores every detail may become harder to search. A system that is very secure may require extra steps from the user.
These choices are called trade-offs.
System design is not only about knowing the parts. It is about choosing which qualities matter most for the problem in front of you.

A banking system cares deeply about correctness and security. A video streaming system cares deeply about speed and smooth playback. A classroom quiz app may care most about simplicity and ease of use.
Good designers explain their trade-offs clearly, because every design is a set of decisions.
Modern computers usually greet us with icons, windows, buttons, and a mouse pointer.
But computers did not begin that way.
For a long time, using a computer meant typing instructions as text.
There was no desktop to click around. You told the machine what to do by writing a command and pressing Enter.
This older style of using a computer is still important, because underneath the friendly screen, computers still respond to precise instructions.
A command line is a place where you control a computer by typing commands.
Instead of clicking a folder, you type a command to move into it.
Instead of dragging a file, you type a command to move it.
Instead of opening a program from an icon, you type the program's name.
The command line looks plain, but it gives direct access to the computer's basic actions: move, list, read, create, copy, rename, delete, and run.
When a command-line computer is ready, it shows a prompt.
The prompt is the computer's way of saying, "I am waiting for your instruction."
You type a command after the prompt, then press Enter.
The computer reads the command, tries to do what you asked, and then shows the prompt again.
That loop is simple: wait, read, act, respond, wait again.
A lot of computing is built from that same pattern.
A command is not magic. It is usually a small program with a specific job.
One command lists files. Another changes folder. Another copies data. Another starts a program.
When you type a command, the computer looks for a program with that name.
If it finds one, it runs it. If it does not, it tells you the command was not recognized.
This is why command-line computing feels strict. The computer cannot guess as freely as a person can. It needs the command to be written in a form it understands.
Before you can control a computer with commands, you need to understand where things live.
A file is a named piece of stored information. It might contain text, a picture, music, code, or settings.
A folder is a container that can hold files and other folders.
The filesystem is the organized map of all those files and folders.
A mouse lets you explore that map visually. The command line lets you move through the same map by typing.
At any moment, the command line has a current location.
That location is the folder you are standing in.
The command `pwd` means "print working directory." It shows your current folder.
On Windows, the similar command is often `cd` by itself, which prints the current folder.
This matters because many commands act on the folder where you are currently standing.
Before you change, copy, or delete anything, it helps to ask the computer, "Where am I?"
Once you know where you are, the next question is, "What is here?"
The command `ls` lists the files and folders in the current location.
On Windows, the older command is `dir`.
These commands are the text version of opening a folder and looking inside.
They do not usually change anything. They simply show what exists.
Looking before acting is one of the safest habits in command-line work.
To move through the filesystem, you use `cd`.
`cd` means "change directory." A directory is another word for a folder.
If you type `cd Documents`, you move into the Documents folder, if it exists where you are.
If you type `cd ..`, you move one level up to the parent folder.
This is like walking into a folder or stepping back out of it.
The command line has no mouse pointer, so your current folder is your position.
Sometimes you do not need to open a full app to see what is inside a text file.
The command `cat filename` prints the contents of a file on the screen.
On Windows, `type filename` does a similar job.
If the file is short, the whole thing appears at once.
If the file is long, it may rush past too quickly, so people often use tools that let them scroll through it.
Reading files from the command line is useful because many computer settings, logs, and programs are stored as text.
The command line can also create new places to store work.
The command `mkdir notes` creates a folder called notes.
`mkdir` means "make directory."
After creating it, you can move into it with `cd notes`.
This is the command-line version of choosing "New Folder."
Creating folders is how you begin organizing work before files start piling up.
Two common actions are copying a file and moving a file.
Copying keeps the original and creates another version somewhere else.
Moving changes where the file lives. It can also be used to rename a file.
The command `cp old.txt new.txt` copies a file on many systems.
The command `mv old.txt new-name.txt` moves or renames a file on many systems.
On Windows, similar commands are `copy` for copying and `move` or `ren` for moving and renaming.
Some commands are safe because they only show information.
Deleting is different because it changes what exists.
On many systems, `rm filename` removes a file.
On Windows, `del filename` removes a file.
Command-line deletion may not behave like dragging something to a recycle bin. It can be immediate.
That is why careful users check their current folder and list the files before deleting anything.
A command line is not only for managing files. It can run programs too.
If a program is available to the command line, typing its name can start it.
For example, typing `python` may start Python. Typing `node` may start Node.js. Typing `git` may run Git.
Sometimes you give the program extra information after its name.
In `python script.py`, the command is `python`, and `script.py` is the file you want Python to run.
This is how typed commands become a way to control larger tools.
Many commands can be adjusted by adding extra words after them.
These extra words are called arguments or options.
An argument usually tells the command what to act on, such as a file or folder name.
An option changes how the command behaves.
For example, `ls` lists files, while `ls -l` asks for a more detailed list on many systems.
A command is like a verb. The arguments and options tell it what to act on and how to act.
Nobody memorizes every command perfectly.
Command-line tools usually include ways to ask for help.
Many commands understand `--help`, such as `git --help` or `python --help`.
On many Unix-style systems, `man command` opens the manual page for a command.
On Windows PowerShell, `Get-Help command` can explain how a command works.
Learning the command line is not about memorizing everything. It is about knowing how to ask the computer what a command can do.
The command line may look old, but it is not obsolete.
Developers, system administrators, data analysts, security teams, and engineers still use typed commands every day.
Text commands are precise. They can be repeated, saved, shared, automated, and combined.
A graphical screen is good for seeing and choosing. A command line is good for giving exact instructions.
Learning commands also reveals something important about computers: the friendly screen is an interface, not the whole machine.
Underneath the icons and buttons, the computer is still a system waiting for instructions it can understand.

boards.title: A matrix is a rectangular array

tags.concept: A matrix is a rectangular array
tags.subject: maths

layers: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns as one mathematical object.
It may look like a small table, but in mathematics the arrangement is part of the object itself, not decoration.
Each position in the array matters. Moving a number to a different row or column can change the matrix and its meaning.
A spreadsheet can help with the first visual idea, but a matrix is not defined by software, labels, or cells.
The useful definition is this: a matrix is one structured object whose entries are organized by row and column position.

boards.title: Entries have row-column positions
layers: Each value inside a matrix is called an entry, and every entry has a position determined by its row and column.
Mathematicians usually name entries with indices. The notation a_{3,2} means the entry in row 3, column 2 of matrix A.
The row number is written first, then the column number. This order is part of the notation and should not be swapped.
Row 2, column 3 and row 3, column 2 are different positions, even if the same number appears in both places.
Once the address system is clear, a matrix becomes organized information rather than a block of disconnected symbols on a page.

boards.title: Matrix size is rows by columns

tags.concept: Matrix size is rows by columns
tags.subject: maths

layers: The size of a matrix is given by its number of rows followed by its number of columns, in that order.
A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is called a 2 \times 3 matrix, read as two by three.
A 3 \times 2 matrix also contains six entries, but it has a different shape and therefore behaves differently in operations.
Matrix dimensions are not decoration. They decide which operations are possible and how the result of an operation will be shaped.
This is why matrices with the same number of entries can still be different mathematical objects with different uses and meanings.

boards.title: Matrix addition matches entries
layers: Two matrices can be added only when they have the same dimensions: the same number of rows and the same number of columns.
Addition is done entry by entry. The entry in row 1, column 1 adds to the entry in row 1, column 1.
The same pairing continues across the entire matrix, so every position in the first matrix matches one position in the second.
If the dimensions do not match, there is no complete row-column pairing, so matrix addition is not defined for those matrices.
The operation respects structure. Matrices add cleanly only when their shapes line up exactly from the first entry to the last.

boards.title: Matrices can represent data
layers: A matrix can represent data whenever information can be arranged in rows and columns with consistent meaning across the whole array.
A black-and-white image, for example, can be represented as a matrix where each entry records the brightness of one pixel.
A value such as 0 may represent black, 255 may represent white, and values between them represent grey levels of brightness.
The matrix is not the picture itself. It is a numerical representation that a computer can store, process, and transform.
This is one reason matrices appear in imaging, statistics, maps, networks, scientific measurement, engineering, economics, and numerical computation across many fields.

boards.title: Matrices can represent transformations
layers: A matrix can also represent a transformation, meaning a systematic action that sends points or vectors to new positions in space.
For example, the matrix \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} doubles the x-coordinate and leaves the y-coordinate unchanged.
Under that transformation, the point (3,4) becomes (6,4) because the horizontal coordinate is stretched by a factor of 2.
In this setting, the entries of the matrix describe how space is stretched, compressed, reflected, rotated, or sheared by the transformation.
This gives matrices a second major role: they can store data, but they can also describe actions on data or space.

boards.title: The identity matrix leaves objects unchanged

tags.concept: The identity matrix leaves objects unchanged
tags.subject: maths

layers: The identity matrix is the matrix version of doing nothing to a vector or point during a transformation in space.
In two dimensions, the identity matrix is \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, and it sends (x,y) back to (x,y).
It plays a role similar to the number 1 in multiplication, because applying it leaves the object unchanged after the operation.
The identity matrix matters because transformations need a clear baseline: the transformation that changes nothing at all to the object.
Once matrices are treated as transformations, the identity matrix becomes the neutral element among those transformations under matrix multiplication in algebra.

boards.title: Rotation can be written as a matrix

tags.concept: Rotation can be written as a matrix
tags.subject: maths

layers: A rotation matrix represents a turn around the origin using entries arranged in a specific pattern inside the matrix itself.
A 90^\circ counterclockwise rotation sends (1,0) to (0,1) and is represented by \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
More general rotation matrices use sine and cosine because those functions describe circular movement around the origin at different angles.
This is where trigonometry and matrices connect: trigonometry describes the turn, and the matrix applies it consistently to every point.
The spreadsheet comparison is only the entrance. A matrix begins as an array, then becomes a language for data and transformation.

boards.title: Exponents are compact multiplication
layers: An exponent is a compact way to write repeated multiplication, where the base is reused as a factor a specific number of times.
For example, 2^4 means 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2. The base is 2, and the exponent is 4.
The notation matters because multiplication chains become difficult to read once the number of repeated factors grows beyond a few terms.
Exponents keep the structure visible. They show both the repeated number and the length of the repetition in one expression.
Once exponents are read this way, the laws of exponents become patterns in multiplication rather than separate facts to memorize.

boards.title: Multiplying powers adds exponents
layers: When two powers have the same base, multiplying them joins their repeated multiplication chains into one longer chain of matching factors.
The expression 3^2 \times 3^4 means two factors of 3 followed by four more factors of 3 in the same product.
Altogether, there are six factors of 3, so the product is 3^6 rather than a new kind of operation.
This is why the exponent law says a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n} when the base is the same.
The base does not change. Only the count of repeated factors changes, because the two multiplication chains have been joined together.

boards.title: Negative exponents mean reciprocal
layers: A negative exponent does not make the final value negative. It changes the position of the power inside a fraction.
For example, 2^{-3} means \frac{1}{2^3}, which equals \frac{1}{8} after the power in the denominator is evaluated.
This extends the ordinary exponent pattern below zero, where each step downward divides by the base again instead of multiplying.
Positive exponents move upward by repeated multiplication. Negative exponents move the same pattern downward by repeated division through reciprocal powers.
Negative exponents are therefore a compact notation for reciprocal powers, especially when very small quantities need to be written cleanly.

boards.title: Fractional exponents are roots
layers: Fractional exponents connect powers and roots, so roots become part of the same notation rather than a separate mathematical language.
The denominator of the exponent tells which root is being taken. For example, x^{1/2} means \sqrt{x}, the square root.
Similarly, x^{1/3} means the cube root of x, because cubing reverses the cube-root operation and returns to x.
More generally, x^{1/n} means the number that must be raised to the power n to produce x again.
This notation lets powers and roots combine smoothly, which becomes important in algebra, graphs, physics, and rate formulas involving change.

boards.title: Exponential growth multiplies
layers: Linear growth adds the same amount each step, while exponential growth multiplies by the same factor at every step instead.
A doubling pattern goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Each amount is multiplied by 2 to produce the next amount.
The early values can look small, but repeated multiplication compounds quickly because each new value becomes the base for the next step.
That is why exponential graphs can appear almost flat at first, then rise sharply once the multiplied values become large.
Compound interest, population growth, viral spread, and chain reactions all use this structure of repeated multiplication over time and scale.

boards.title: Exponential decay shrinks by a factor

tags.concept: Exponential decay shrinks by a factor
tags.subject: maths

layers: Exponential decay is the same structure as exponential growth, but each step keeps only a fixed fraction of the previous amount.
If a quantity halves each hour, 80 becomes 40, then 20, then 10, with the same factor applied each time.
The amount does not fall by equal subtraction. It falls by equal proportion, which makes the decrease smaller as the quantity shrinks.
This is why decay curves drop quickly at first, then flatten as there is less remaining quantity to lose at later stages.
Radioactive decay, cooling, capacitor discharge, and medicine leaving the bloodstream can all be modeled with exponential decay over time and quantity.

boards.title: A logarithm asks what power
layers: A logarithm reverses the question asked by an exponent. It asks which power was needed to produce a given number.
If 10^3 = 1000, then \log_{10}(1000) = 3, because 3 is the exponent that produces 1000 from base 10.
The base of the logarithm tells which number was being powered. The answer is the exponent attached to that base.
Logarithms are not a new kind of arithmetic. They are a way of reading exponential statements from the other direction.
This makes logarithms useful whenever an unknown value is sitting in the exponent instead of beside the base in an equation.

boards.title: Logs turn multiplication into addition
layers: Logarithms connect multiplication and addition because multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents rather than multiplying them directly.
This is the reason \log(ab) = \log(a) + \log(b), as long as the logarithms use the same base throughout.
The logarithm is reading the exponent hidden behind each number, so multiplying the numbers becomes adding those hidden exponents instead.
This property made logarithms powerful calculation tools long before electronic calculators, because hard multiplication could be converted into easier addition.
The same idea still matters in algebra, data scales, signal measurement, and any situation where multiplicative change needs to be compared.

boards.title: The natural base e
layers: The number e appears when growth is compounded continuously, meaning the compounding is treated as happening without separate time jumps.
Its decimal begins near 2.718, but the exact decimal is less important than the continuous-change behavior it represents in formulas.
The function e^x is special because its rate of change matches its own value at every point on the graph.
That property makes e central in calculus, especially when describing growth, decay, cooling, charging, and many physical systems mathematically over time.
In this sense, e is not chosen for convenience. It appears naturally when change depends on the current amount present.

boards.title: Exponents and logs are mirrors
layers: Exponential functions and logarithmic functions undo each other, so each one reverses the action of the other in equations and graphs.
If an exponential function sends 3 to 1000, the matching logarithm sends 1000 back to 3 again as its exponent.
On a coordinate graph, inverse functions mirror each other across the line y = x, swapping inputs and outputs between axes.
This inverse relationship is what allows logarithms to solve equations where the unknown value appears in the exponent instead of the base.
Exponents describe repeated multiplication moving forward. Logarithms recover the exponent that created the result from a chosen base in reverse.

boards.title: Charge is the thing that moves

layers.text: Electricity begins with charge. Charge is a property of particles that lets them push and pull through electric forces.
Electrons carry negative charge. Protons carry positive charge. In metal wires, the mobile charges are mostly electrons.
A circuit is not made from mysterious energy fluid. It is organised charge movement through a conducting path.
Once charge can move, current, voltage, and resistance become easier to understand.
Electric current measures how much charge passes a point each second.
The unit is the ampere. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passing each second.
In circuit diagrams, current is treated as flowing around the loop through every component on its path.
Current is not used up by a bulb. Energy is transferred, but charge keeps circulating.
Voltage tells how much energy each unit of charge gains or loses between two points.
A battery gives charges energy. A bulb or resistor transfers that energy into light, heat, or another form.
Voltage is measured across components, not through them.
Thinking of voltage as energy per charge is cleaner than thinking of it only as a push.
Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes the movement of charge.
A thin wire, long wire, hot wire, or poor conductor usually has higher resistance.
Resistance does not destroy charge. It transfers electrical energy into other forms, often heat.
This is why resistors are useful: they control current and manage energy transfer.
Ohm law links voltage, current, and resistance with a simple relationship: V = IR.
If resistance stays fixed, increasing voltage increases current.
If voltage stays fixed, increasing resistance reduces current.
The equation is simple, but it becomes the working grammar of basic circuit analysis.
In a series circuit, components sit one after another on a single path.
The same current passes through every component because there is nowhere else for the charge to go.
The supply voltage is shared between the components.
Add more resistors in series, and the total resistance rises. The current usually falls.
In a parallel circuit, the current has more than one path.
Each branch gets the full supply voltage, because each branch connects across the same two points.
The total current splits between branches and then recombines.
This is why home wiring uses parallel branches: one device can turn off while others keep working.
Electrical power tells how quickly electrical energy is transferred into another form.
The basic equation is P = IV: power equals current times voltage.
A high-power heater transfers energy quickly. A small LED transfers energy much more slowly.
Power connects circuit measurements to real effects: heat, light, motion, and sound.
Kirchhoff current rule says charge does not pile up at a junction.
Current entering a junction must equal current leaving it.
Kirchhoff voltage rule says energy is conserved around a closed loop.
Together, these rules turn messy circuits into bookkeeping: charge in, charge out, energy gained, energy spent.
A capacitor stores energy by separating positive and negative charge on two conducting plates.
It does not store charge by creating extra charge. It separates charge already present in the circuit.
When connected, a capacitor can charge, hold energy briefly, and then discharge.
That makes capacitors useful for timing, smoothing, filtering, and short bursts of stored electrical energy.

boards.title: Isotopes are the same element with different mass

layers.text: Atoms of the same element always have the same number of protons.
Isotopes are atoms of that element with different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon because both have six protons.
The neutron difference changes mass, but it does not change the element identity.
Electrons sit around the nucleus in energy levels often called shells.
The outer shell matters most in ordinary chemistry.
Atoms react because their outer electrons can be lost, gained, or shared.
So chemical behaviour is mostly a story about the outer shell.
An atom becomes an ion when it loses or gains electrons.
Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion becomes positive.
Gaining electrons gives more electrons than protons, so the ion becomes negative.
The nucleus has not changed. The charge changed because the electron count changed.

boards.title: Ionic bonding is give and take

layers.text: Ionic bonding begins when one atom transfers electrons to another.
The metal atom usually loses electrons and becomes a positive ion.
The non-metal atom usually gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.
The opposite charges attract, pulling the ions into a repeating giant lattice.
Covalent bonding happens when atoms share pairs of electrons.
This usually happens between non-metal atoms that both need outer-shell electrons.
A shared pair is attracted to both nuclei, holding the atoms together.
Water, carbon dioxide, methane, glucose, and DNA all depend on covalent bonding.

boards.title: Metallic bonding creates a sea of electrons

layers.text: In a metal, outer electrons are not locked to one atom.
They move through a lattice of positive metal ions.
This sea of mobile electrons holds the structure together.
It also explains why metals conduct electricity, conduct heat, and bend without shattering.

boards.title: Molecular shape comes from electron repulsion

layers.text: Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other.
They arrange themselves as far apart as possible in three-dimensional space.
That simple repulsion predicts shapes such as linear, bent, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral.
Shape matters because molecules react and interact according to their actual geometry.
A covalent bond can share electrons unevenly.
The atom pulling harder becomes slightly negative, while the other side becomes slightly positive.
This creates polarity, a small separation of charge inside the molecule.
Polarity helps explain boiling points, solubility, and why water is such an effective solvent.
A chemical reaction does not create atoms from nothing.
It breaks old bonds, rearranges atoms, and forms new bonds.
The substances at the start are reactants. The substances formed are products.
The atom count is conserved, but the arrangement changes. That is why new substances appear.
A chemical equation must have the same number of each atom on both sides.
Balancing does not change formulas. It changes how many formula units take part.
Coefficients go in front of formulas because they count whole particles.
Balanced equations are conservation of matter written in chemical language.

Temperature and heat sound similar, but they answer different questions. Temperature describes how energetically particles are moving on average. Heat describes energy transferred because one place is warmer than another.
A tiny spark can be extremely hot but carry very little energy. A warm bath has a lower temperature, but far more particles, so it can transfer much more heat.
Temperature is measured in kelvin or degrees Celsius. Heat is measured in joules, the same unit used for energy and work.
This distinction matters everywhere in thermal physics. A thermometer reads temperature. It does not tell the full amount of thermal energy available to move, warm, melt, or burn something.

boards.title: Kelvin starts at the cold limit

layers.text: Celsius is convenient for daily life: water freezes near 0°C and boils near 100°C at normal pressure. Physics usually needs a scale with a deeper zero.
The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature. The size of one kelvin is the same as one Celsius degree, but the starting point is different.
The conversion is simple: T in kelvin = T in Celsius + 273.15. Room temperature is about 20°C, or about 293 K.
Gas laws and engine formulas use kelvin because they depend on absolute temperature. Using Celsius inside those equations can produce negative pressures or volumes that make no physical sense.
Most materials expand when heated. Their particles vibrate more strongly, and the average spacing between neighbouring particles becomes slightly larger.
The effect is small for a spoon or a coin, but it becomes serious for railway tracks, bridges, pipes, and power lines stretched across long distances.
Linear expansion is written as ΔL = alpha L0 ΔT. The expansion depends on the material, the original length, and the temperature change.
Engineers leave expansion gaps because the material will move whether anyone wants it to or not. Ignoring thermal expansion can bend rails, crack concrete, and jam moving parts.
Different materials need different amounts of energy to change temperature. Water is especially stubborn: it takes a lot of energy to warm it even by one degree.
That is why a metal spoon heats quickly in hot tea while the tea itself changes temperature slowly. Metals often have lower specific heat capacity than water.
The key equation is Q = mcΔT. Heat transferred equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change.
Specific heat explains kettles, cooking pans, car radiators, oceans, and climate buffering. A material with high specific heat can absorb a lot of energy before its temperature shifts much.
When ice melts, its temperature stays at 0°C until the melting is complete. Energy is still entering, but it is not raising the temperature.
That energy is used to loosen the structure holding the solid together. During boiling, energy separates liquid molecules into gas instead of simply making them warmer.
The equation for a phase change is Q = mL. The symbol L is latent heat, the energy needed per kilogram to change state.
Latent heat is why steam can burn badly. Steam at 100°C releases a large extra store of energy when it condenses back into liquid water.
Calorimetry is the practice of measuring heat transfer. The usual setup is simple: put warm and cool things together, insulate them, and watch the final temperature.
A hot metal block dropped into cooler water loses heat. The water gains heat. If the cup is well insulated, those amounts should balance.
The bookkeeping idea is heat lost = heat gained. In symbols, the total heat change across the insulated system is approximately zero.
This is how unknown specific heat capacities are measured. It also teaches the habit thermodynamics uses constantly: track where energy enters, where it leaves, and where it is stored.

boards.title: Matter changes state by rearranging particles

layers.text: Solid, liquid, and gas are not different kinds of substance. They are different arrangements and motions of the same particles.
In a solid, particles vibrate around fixed positions. In a liquid, they stay close but slide past each other. In a gas, they spread out and move freely.
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of this random motion. Heating usually makes the particle motion stronger.
The particle model explains melting, boiling, evaporation, diffusion, and pressure. It is simple, but it gives a microscopic picture behind the everyday behaviour of matter.

boards.title: An ideal gas is a useful simplification

layers.text: Real gases are complicated. Molecules have size, attract each other slightly, and behave differently near condensation. The ideal gas model strips those details away.
It treats gas particles as tiny points moving randomly, colliding elastically, and exerting no forces except during collisions.
No gas is perfectly ideal. Many gases behave close to ideal when pressure is low and temperature is reasonably high.
The model is valuable because it turns a messy molecular swarm into clear relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of gas.

boards.title: The gas laws show simple patterns

layers.text: The early gas laws each freeze one variable and watch how the others change. That makes the pattern easier to see.
Boyle law says that at constant temperature, squeezing a gas into a smaller volume raises its pressure. A bicycle pump is the everyday version.
Charles law says that at constant pressure, heating a gas makes its volume increase. The pressure law says that in a fixed container, heating raises pressure.
Together, these laws say gases are not random in their large-scale behaviour. Pressure, volume, and absolute temperature move in predictable linked ways.

boards.title: PV = nRT ties the gas together

layers.text: The ideal gas equation combines the gas laws into one compact relationship: PV = nRT.
P is pressure, V is volume, n is the amount of gas in moles, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature in kelvin.
Given any three of those quantities, the fourth can be found. The equation also helps reason qualitatively before calculating.
If a sealed tyre warms up, volume is almost fixed and n is fixed, so pressure rises. The equation is not only arithmetic; it is a map of cause and effect.
A gas pushes on its container because its molecules keep hitting the walls. Each collision is tiny, but the number of collisions is enormous.
Heating the gas makes molecules move faster. Faster molecules hit the walls more often and with greater impulse, so the pressure increases if the volume is fixed.
Kinetic theory links the microscopic view to the macroscopic gas law. The average molecular kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature.
This is the bridge from invisible motion to readable measurements. A pressure gauge is indirectly reading the violence of molecular impacts inside the container.

boards.title: The first law keeps energy honest

layers.text: The first law of thermodynamics is conservation of energy applied to heat, work, and internal energy.
A gas can gain energy by being heated. It can lose energy by pushing a piston outward and doing work on the outside world.
One common sign convention writes ΔU = Q - W. Internal energy rises when heat is added, and falls when the system does work.
The law prevents magical thinking. Energy does not appear or vanish inside an engine, kettle, refrigerator, or body. It changes account: heat, work, or internal storage.
Thermodynamics cares not only about the starting and ending states, but also about the path taken between them.
An isothermal process keeps temperature constant. An adiabatic process exchanges no heat. An isobaric process keeps pressure constant. An isochoric process keeps volume constant.
These names are labels for controlled changes. They make gas problems readable by saying which quantity is being held still.
On a pressure-volume diagram, the area under the curve represents work done by the gas. The shape of the path matters, not just the endpoints.
Some processes happen naturally in one direction. Hot coffee cools in a room. It does not gather scattered heat from the room and become hotter by itself.
The second law says entropy tends to increase in an isolated system. Energy becomes more spread out and less available for organised work.
Entropy is often introduced as disorder, but the sharper idea is energy dispersal and the number of microscopic arrangements available.
This is why time has a thermal arrow. Broken cups do not reassemble, perfume spreads through a room, and useful energy gradually becomes harder to recover.

boards.title: Heat engines turn heat into work

layers.text: A heat engine takes energy from a hot source, turns part of it into useful work, and dumps the rest into a colder place.
Car engines, steam turbines, and power stations all follow this basic pattern. Heat enters, work comes out, and waste heat must leave.
The Carnot limit gives the best possible efficiency between two temperatures: eta = 1 - Tc/Th, with temperatures measured in kelvin.
No real engine reaches that ideal. The point is not to build perfection, but to know the ceiling. Temperature difference is what makes heat engines possible.

boards.title: A computer is a filing system with a brain attached

layers.text: Before code, cloud, or AI, a computer has to keep things somewhere. A file is a named block of data. A folder is just a way to give many files an address.
That sounds ordinary, which is why it is easy to skip. Most useful computer work begins with knowing where the inputs live, where the outputs should go, and which copy is the real one.
Text, images, spreadsheets, videos, programs, and model weights all become files at some point. The machine does not see a school report or a photograph. It sees bytes with a name and a path.
People who handle computers well are often good at this unglamorous layer. They name things clearly, keep versions separate, and can find the exact artifact a tool is supposed to read.
A file path is the address of a file inside the machine. It tells the operating system which drive, folder, subfolder, and filename to follow.
When software says it cannot find a file, it is usually not confused about the file itself. It is looking in the wrong place, or the name does not match exactly.
There are absolute paths, which start from the root of the system, and relative paths, which start from the folder the program is currently standing in.
That one idea explains many beginner errors. The program is not reading thoughts. It is walking an address, one folder at a time.

boards.title: The command line is the old control room

layers.text: A graphical app lets us click visible controls. A shell lets us type commands directly to the operating system.
The command line feels bare because it removes the buttons. In exchange, it gives exact control: list these files, enter this folder, run this program, copy this output.
Modern AI tools make the shell more valuable, not less. A model can suggest a command, but the user still needs to know what folder it will affect and what output to expect.
The first useful shell skill is calm reading. What command ran? From which folder? What did the error actually say?

boards.title: Programs are tools that expect inputs

layers.text: A program is a machine made of instructions. It waits for inputs, follows its rules, and produces outputs.
The input might be a file, a typed command, a web request, a mouse click, a sensor reading, or a question sent to an AI model.
The output might be a saved image, a row in a database, a page on a screen, a sound from a speaker, or another file passed to the next tool.
Once this pattern is visible, software becomes less mysterious. Many systems are just chains of small programs handing results to one another.
Computers work best when data has a predictable shape. A spreadsheet uses rows and columns. JSON uses names, brackets, lists, and values.
Human notes can be loose. Software needs stricter habits. If one record says price and another says cost, a program may treat them as different fields.
This is why forms, tables, schemas, and validation exist. They keep the data boring enough for a machine to read without guessing.
AI can help clean messy data, but clean structure still wins. A neat table beats a clever apology from a model.

boards.title: An API is a contract between programs

layers.text: An API is a published way for one program to talk to another. It says what can be asked, what must be sent, and what comes back.
A weather app does not own every thermometer in the world. It sends a request to a weather service and receives data in a known format.
The same idea powers payments, maps, login systems, AI models, shipping labels, calendars, and almost every modern web product.
Good API thinking is precise. Which endpoint? Which method? Which fields? Which error code?
An app without storage forgets everything when it closes. A database gives the app memory.
Users, scores, messages, orders, lessons, subscriptions, and progress all become records. Each record has fields that can be created, read, changed, or deleted.
The hard part is deciding what should be remembered. Store too little and the app cannot serve the user. Store too much and the system becomes expensive, risky, and hard to change.
A serious product is often a clean interface sitting on top of a careful database design.

boards.title: A model predicts the next useful piece

layers.text: A modern language model reads a sequence of tokens and predicts what should come next. Tokens are small chunks of text, sometimes whole words, sometimes pieces of words.

During training, the model sees enormous amounts of text and adjusts billions of internal numbers. Those numbers become a compressed map of patterns in language, code, facts, style, and reasoning traces.
When a prompt arrives, the model is not opening a private library of perfect answers. It is using those learned patterns to continue the sequence in a useful direction.
That is why wording matters. A vague prompt gives weak steering. A clear task, context, constraints, and examples give the model something firmer to follow.

boards.title: A prompt is a work order

layers.text: A prompt is not a magic sentence. It is a work order for a machine that can read, write, transform, classify, plan, and generate code.
Good work orders name the job. Summarize this contract for a non-lawyer. Find contradictions in this spreadsheet. Rewrite this lesson for a fifteen-year-old without dumbing it down.
The prompt should also name the materials. Paste the relevant text, describe the audience, specify the format, and say what counts as success.
When the output is poor, the best response is often not anger. Tighten the work order.
An AI model can only use what fits inside its context window and what its tools can retrieve. Context is the working memory of the conversation.
If the needed file, rule, date, table, or decision is missing, the model may guess. It may sound confident because language can be fluent even when the ground is thin.
Strong AI work is mostly context management: provide the right source, remove stale instructions, keep decisions recorded, and ask the model to cite what it used.
The better the context, the less the model has to invent.

boards.title: Search and AI solve different problems

layers.text: Search is good at finding existing pages. AI is good at transforming material once the right material is present.
For a current fact, search should win. Prices, laws, model names, sports scores, library versions, and company policies can change after a model was trained.
For synthesis, AI becomes useful. It can compare notes, draft options, spot missing steps, write code, turn rough bullets into a lesson, or explain an error message.
The skilled habit is choosing the right tool first. Lookup before claiming. Transform after grounding.
An embedding turns a piece of text, image, or audio into a long list of numbers. Similar meanings land near each other in that number space.
This is how a system can find a document about refunds even if the user searches for getting money back. The words differ. The meaning is close.
Vector search is built on this idea. Store embeddings for many documents, embed the query, then retrieve the nearest matches.
Many useful AI apps are built from this quiet trick: find the relevant source first, then ask the model to answer from it.

boards.title: RAG gives a model papers on the desk

layers.text: RAG means retrieval augmented generation. The name is clumsy, but the idea is plain: fetch relevant documents before asking the model to answer.
A support bot can retrieve the exact refund policy, shipping rule, or troubleshooting guide, then write a response using that source.
This reduces guessing because the model is not relying only on memory from training. It has the current material sitting in the prompt.
RAG does not make truth automatic. The retrieved source can be old, incomplete, or wrong. The system still needs good documents and checks.
Automation begins when a repeated decision is written down clearly enough for a machine to perform.
If an invoice arrives, extract the amount, check the supplier, save the PDF, update the sheet, and send a message if something looks unusual.
None of those steps is glamorous. Together, they remove hours of dull work and reduce the chance that a tired person misses a detail.
The best automations start small. One trigger. One action. One check that proves the result is right.
An AI agent is usually a loop. Read the goal, decide the next step, use a tool, inspect the result, then decide again.
The tools might include a browser, a code editor, a terminal, a database, a calendar, or an image generator. The model supplies judgment between tool calls.
This makes agents powerful and risky. A bad instruction can repeat, overwrite, spend money, leak data, or confidently finish the wrong task.
Good agent design gives narrow permissions, visible logs, stop points, and tests. Freedom is earned one tool at a time.
AI tools often run on servers. That means a pasted document may leave the local machine and travel to another company's infrastructure.
Some tasks are safe to outsource. Some require removing names, account numbers, addresses, private keys, passwords, medical details, or client material first.
The useful question is simple: would this text be acceptable in the wrong inbox? If the answer is no, treat it carefully before uploading.
Privacy is not fear of technology. It is knowing where the data goes.
Git is a memory system for a folder of work. It records snapshots called commits, each with a message explaining what changed.
This matters because real projects move through mistakes. A feature breaks. A file is renamed. A teammate edits the same area. Git keeps a trail.
Branches let people try work separately before merging it back. Pull requests create a place to review the change before it becomes part of the main project.
In the AI era, Git becomes even more important. Fast code generation needs a strong undo history.

boards.title: Deployment turns code into a service

layers.text: Code on a laptop is private. Deployment puts that code on a server where other people can reach it.
A deployment platform usually builds the project, copies the finished files or server code, assigns an address, and routes web traffic to it.
When a site goes live, the problem changes. It now needs environment variables, monitoring, rollbacks, backups, security rules, and a way to ship fixes without panic.
Launch is not a ceremony. It is the moment the computer has to behave while strangers are watching.

boards.title: Logs are the machine speaking back

layers.text: When software fails, it often leaves a trail. Logs record what happened: requests, warnings, errors, timings, missing files, rejected permissions, and failed assumptions.
A beginner sees a wall of red text. An engineer scans for the first real error, the file name, the line number, and the operation that failed.
AI can help read logs, but it needs the exact message. Paraphrasing an error usually removes the clue that matters.
Debugging is not guessing in a panic. It is asking the machine what it saw, then believing the evidence.

boards.title: The new computer skill is orchestration

layers.text: The valuable computer user is changing. Memorising every command matters less than understanding how tools fit together.
A strong operator can gather data, structure it, ask an AI model for help, verify the result, save the work, ship the change, and recover when something breaks.
That is orchestration. The human sets the goal, chooses the tools, checks the evidence, and keeps responsibility for the result.
Computers are becoming more capable. That makes fundamentals more useful, not less.

boards.title: The machine still only has switches

layers.text: When a chatbot replies in smooth English, it can feel as if the computer has finally learned language directly. The old lesson still holds.
Inside the hardware, everything is still represented by bits. A 1 means one electrical state. A 0 means another. The machine moves those states, not meanings.
English has to be translated before the hardware can touch it. Letters, words, images, and sounds become numbers, then those numbers become patterns of bits in memory.
AI is built on that foundation. The surface feels conversational, but underneath it is encoded data, arithmetic, memory, and circuits switching at enormous speed.

boards.title: The unit circle extends trigonometry
layers: Right triangles give a useful starting point for trigonometry, but they only handle acute angles inside a triangle with fixed sides.
The unit circle extends the same ideas to every angle by placing a circle of radius 1 around the origin.
An angle \theta is measured from the positive x-axis to a radius ending at a point on the circle.
The x-coordinate of that point is \cos\theta, and the y-coordinate is \sin\theta for that angle on the circle.
With this definition, sine and cosine can describe turning, rotation, waves, and repeating motion beyond right-triangle geometry alone in many contexts.

boards.title: Special angles come from geometry
layers: The exact values for 30^\circ, 45^\circ, and 60^\circ come from two standard triangles, not from isolated table entries.
Cutting a square along its diagonal creates a 45^\circ-45^\circ-90^\circ triangle with two equal shorter sides.
That equality explains why \sin45^\circ and \cos45^\circ have the same value on the unit circle and in right triangles.
Cutting an equilateral triangle in half creates a 30^\circ-60^\circ-90^\circ triangle with side ratio 1:\sqrt{3}:2.
These two triangles generate the familiar exact values, so the table becomes a summary of geometry rather than memorized data.

boards.title: Exact values preserve structure
layers: Trigonometry has a small set of exact reference values for sine, cosine, and tangent at common angles used repeatedly in problems.
The usual reference angles are 0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, and 90^\circ, measured from the positive x-axis.
Along these angles, sine rises from 0 to 1, while cosine follows the same pattern in reverse order across the table.
Tangent is defined by \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} wherever \cos\theta is not zero, so division is valid.
Exact values such as \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, and \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} keep the geometry visible.

boards.title: Sine and cosine form waves
layers: As a point moves around the unit circle, its vertical coordinate rises, falls, and returns to the same height after one turn.
Plotting that vertical coordinate against the angle produces the sine wave, one of the basic periodic graphs in mathematics and physics.
Cosine comes from the horizontal coordinate, so it follows the same repeating pattern with a different starting position on the graph.
Both graphs have amplitude 1, midline 0, and period 2\pi, meaning they repeat after one full turn around the circle.
Sound, tides, alternating current, pendulum motion, and circular motion all connect to trigonometry through repeating change over time and space.

boards.title: Tangent measures slope and ratio
layers: Tangent behaves differently from sine and cosine because it is not limited to values between -1 and 1 on its graph.
Since \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}, tangent grows very large when \cos\theta gets close to zero in the denominator.
On its graph, tangent has vertical asymptotes where the function is undefined because division by zero would occur there at those angles.
Tangent also measures slope: a line making angle \theta with the positive x-axis has slope \tan\theta in coordinate geometry.
This links trigonometry to gradients, direction, and steepness, not only to side lengths inside triangles or values on circles alone.

boards.title: Radians measure angle by arc length

tags.concept: Radians measure angle by arc length
tags.subject: maths

layers: Degrees are useful for everyday angle measurement, but radians are built from the geometry of the circle itself and its arc lengths.
One radian is the angle formed when the arc length on a circle is equal to the radius of that circle.
A full turn is 2\pi radians, half a turn is \pi radians, and a quarter turn is \frac{\pi}{2} radians.
Radians make circular formulas cleaner because arc length becomes s=r\theta when \theta is measured in radians rather than degrees.
They also make calculus with sine and cosine work naturally, without extra conversion factors attached to the derivatives of these functions.

boards.title: Differentiation finds local slope
layers: A straight line has one slope everywhere, but a curve changes its steepness from point to point along its path.
Differentiation finds the slope of a curve at one chosen point by studying slopes over shrinking intervals around that point.
The average slope between two nearby points is called a secant slope, because the line cuts through the curve between them.
As the second point moves closer to the first, those secant slopes may approach one stable value for the curve.
That limiting value is the derivative, which gives the slope of the tangent line at that point on the curve.

boards.title: The derivative is a limit of change

tags.concept: The derivative is a limit of change
tags.subject: maths

layers: The derivative of a function records how fast the output changes compared with the input at a specific point locally.
In symbols, the derivative can be written as f'(x) or as \frac{dy}{dx} when y=f(x) for the same idea.
The notation \frac{dy}{dx} compares a small change in y with a small change in x near a point.
The derivative becomes exact when that comparison is taken as a limit while the change in x shrinks toward zero.
This is why differentiation belongs after limits: it is built from the limit of shrinking average rates of change near a point.

boards.title: The derivative of x squared
layers: The function y=x^2 gives a clean first example because its slope changes smoothly from point to point along the curve.
Near x=3, the slopes between nearby points on the curve get closer and closer to 6 as the interval shrinks.
This means the tangent line to y=x^2 at x=3 has slope 6 at that exact point, not across an interval.
More generally, the derivative of x^2 is 2x, so the local slope depends on the chosen input value on the graph.
Differentiation turns a function into another function that reports the original function's rate of change at each input value in its domain.

boards.title: The power rule is a shortcut

tags.concept: The power rule is a shortcut
tags.subject: maths

layers: Once the derivative pattern is known, many derivatives do not need to be rebuilt from the limit definition each time.
The power rule says that for x^n, the exponent moves in front and the exponent is reduced by one.
In notation, \frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1} for powers where the rule applies in elementary differentiation and algebra.
For example, the derivative of x^4 is 4x^3, and the derivative of 5x^4 is 20x^3 by the power rule.
Constants by themselves have derivative 0 because a horizontal line has no change in height as x changes at all.

boards.title: Products and quotients need structure
layers: The derivative of a product is not usually the product of the derivatives, because both factors may change together at once.
The product rule accounts for both contributions: one factor changes while the other is held, then the roles switch between factors.
In notation, (fg)'=f'g+fg', where each term captures one part of the product's changing behavior in the calculation of change.
Division has its own pattern, called the quotient rule, because the numerator and denominator affect the fraction differently as they change.
These rules matter whenever changing quantities multiply or divide, including area, revenue, density, ratios, and physical formulas in applications like these.

boards.title: The chain rule handles layers
layers: Many functions are built in layers, where one function acts first and another function acts on its output afterward inside the composition.
The chain rule differentiates the outside layer, then multiplies by the derivative of the inside layer underneath in the composition.
For (3x^2+5)^7, the outside contributes 7(3x^2+5)^6, and the inside contributes 6x from differentiating 3x^2+5.
Multiplying those parts gives the derivative 42x(3x^2+5)^6 for the full layered expression after simplification of the product.
The chain rule matters because layered functions appear in physics, geometry, statistics, optimization, computer-based models, and simulations of real systems.

boards.title: Light can be modelled as rays

layers.text: Light is an electromagnetic wave, but many everyday optical problems can be solved with a simpler model: rays.
A ray is an imaginary line showing the path light takes. In a uniform medium, that path is treated as straight.
The model works well when mirrors, lenses, screens, and openings are much larger than the wavelength of visible light.
That simplification explains pinhole cameras, shadows, mirrors, lenses, prisms, fibre optics, and much of how vision works.
When light hits a smooth mirror, it bounces in a predictable way. The incoming angle equals the outgoing angle.
Both angles are measured from the normal, an imaginary line standing perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact.
A rough surface still obeys the same rule at each tiny patch, but the patches face different directions, so light scatters.
This difference explains why a mirror forms a clear image while paper can be seen from many angles without behaving like a mirror.
A flat mirror seems to place the image behind the glass, even though no light is actually coming from behind it.
The reflected rays enter the eye, and the brain traces them backward in straight lines. Their backward extensions meet behind the mirror.
That image is virtual: it can be seen, but it cannot be caught on a screen placed behind the mirror.
The image sits as far behind the mirror as the object sits in front. Same size, upright, but laterally reversed.
A straw in water looks bent because light changes direction when it crosses from one medium into another.
The cause is speed. Light travels at different speeds in air, water, glass, and other transparent materials.
When light enters a slower medium at an angle, it bends toward the normal. When it enters a faster medium, it bends away.
Refraction is the reason lenses focus, pools look shallower, prisms spread colour, and glasses can correct vision.
Refraction has an exact rule. Snell law connects the two angles with the two refractive indices of the materials.
The equation is n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. The angles are measured from the normal.
If light goes from air into water, the refractive index rises, the speed falls, and the ray bends toward the normal.
Designing lenses, cameras, microscopes, fibre optics, and eye corrections depends on applying this relationship again and again.

boards.title: Lenses focus by bending many rays

layers.text: A lens is a shaped transparent object that bends different rays by different amounts, bringing them together or spreading them apart.
A converging lens is thicker in the middle and can bring parallel rays to a focus. A diverging lens spreads rays outward.
The focal length tells how strongly a lens bends light. Short focal length means strong bending and a focus close to the lens.
Cameras, spectacles, microscopes, telescopes, projectors, and the eye all use this controlled bending to form useful images.

boards.title: The mole is chemistry counting at scale

layers.text: Chemistry needs to count atoms and molecules, but single particles are far too small to count one by one in a lab.
The mole solves that scale problem. One mole means 6.022 × 1023 particles, whether those particles are atoms, ions, or molecules.
It is a counting unit, like a dozen, but built for the atomic world. The number is huge because atoms are tiny.
Once the mole is understood as counting, chemical equations become recipes for particle groups rather than mysterious symbol strings.
No chemist counts a mole of atoms with tweezers. The practical method is to count by mass.
The periodic table gives the molar mass: the mass in grams of one mole of that element or compound.
Carbon has a molar mass close to 12 g/mol. So 12 grams of carbon contains about one mole of carbon atoms.
This turns an invisible count into a measurement a lab balance can handle. Weighing becomes counting.

boards.title: n equals m over M is the bridge

layers.text: The bridge between mass and amount is n = m / M. Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass.
If sodium hydroxide has molar mass 40 g/mol, then 80 grams of it contains 2 moles.
The mass is what sits on the balance. The molar mass comes from the formula and the periodic table.
This equation is one of chemistry's daily workhorses because reactions are planned in moles, not just grams.
The large numbers in a balanced chemical equation are not decoration. They are ratios between reacting amounts.
The equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O says two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen.
Those ratios let a chemist predict how much product can form from the amounts placed in the reaction vessel.
