The usual workflow is mass to moles, mole ratio through the equation, then moles back to mass for the product.

boards.title: One reactant can run out first

layers.text: A reaction stops when one required reactant runs out. The remaining reactants may still be present, but the recipe can no longer continue.
That first exhausted reactant is called the limiting reactant. It limits the maximum amount of product that can be made.
This is like building sandwiches with bread and cheese. Extra cheese does nothing if the bread is gone.
Limiting reactant calculations protect labs and factories from wasting material, overestimating yield, or misunderstanding why a reaction stopped.
Moles also help chemists work backward from measurements to a formula. Mass percentages alone do not show the true particle ratio.
Convert each element's mass into moles, then compare the mole amounts. The simplest whole-number ratio gives the empirical formula.
If the real molecular mass is larger than the empirical formula mass, the empirical formula is multiplied to reach the molecular formula.
This is how an unknown substance can be identified from careful measurements rather than from appearance alone.

boards.title: The Rule Machine
layers: A rule such as "double it and add three" can accept different input numbers without changing the rule itself.
If 2 goes in, 7 comes out. If 5 goes in, 13 comes out. Each input is handled in the same way.
A function is a rule that takes an allowed input and returns a definite output.
The same function can appear in words, in a table, on a graph, or as a formula.
The function is the pairing: each input is connected to its own output.

boards.title: The Graph of a Rule
layers: The rule "double it and add three" can be tested on several input numbers while the rule stays unchanged.
Each input-output pair becomes a point. The input gives the x-position, and the output gives the y-position.
When the points for 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are plotted, they form an ordered pattern rather than scattered marks.
For this rule, the points fall on a straight line because the output rises by the same amount each time.
A graph places the rule on the plane, where its pattern can be seen instead of only calculated.

boards.title: Slope as a Rate
layers: A ramp can rise gently or sharply. In each case, horizontal distance is paired with a change in height.
On a graph, slope measures a similar comparison: how much y changes when x changes by a chosen amount.
If x moves one step right while y rises two steps, the slope of that line is two.
Slope is more than a drawing feature. It is a rate of change built into the line.
The same structure later describes speed, growth, reaction rate, and other quantities that compare one change with another.

boards.title: When a Line Becomes Motion
layers: When time is placed on the x-axis and position on the y-axis, a graph can describe motion.
A flat line means the position is not changing, so the object is stationary during that interval.
A rising straight line means the object is moving steadily away from the starting position as time passes.
The slope of that line is the velocity, because it shows how position changes with time.
A line that describes a number rule can also describe an object changing position over time.

boards.title: The Energy Account
layers: Push a toy car across the floor, and the car can now do things it could not do before the push.
It can roll into a block, climb a small ramp, or scrape along the floor until friction slows it down.
Energy is the account used for the ability to produce motion, heat, lifting, stretching, or some other physical change in matter.
Energy is not a liquid inside the car, but it can be transferred from one object or process to another.
A rolling car, a warm floor, and a lifted weight can be connected by following where the energy transfers during each event.

boards.title: Work Means Force Through Distance
layers: Push a box across the floor. The push changes the box only while the box moves through some distance across the surface.
A person can push against a wall and become tired, even though the wall has not moved through any measurable distance.
In physics, work means a force acting through a distance in the same direction as the motion of the object.
A force alone is not enough, and motion alone is not enough. The force has to act through the motion.
In the simplest case, work is written as W = Fd: force multiplied by distance in the direction of motion on the object.

boards.title: Momentum as Moving Mass
layers: A tennis ball and a bowling ball can roll at the same speed, but stopping them requires very different pushes.
The bowling ball carries more motion to deal with because the same speed is attached to much more mass than the tennis ball.
Momentum is mass times velocity, so it depends on both the amount of matter and the direction of motion, not speed alone.
Because velocity has direction, momentum has direction too. It points in the same direction as the moving object travels through space.
Momentum becomes important in collisions, recoils, explosions, and pushes between objects that act on each other during contact or separation.

boards.title: Stretching the Stop
layers: Catching a fast ball with stiff hands can hurt because the stop happens quickly and the force becomes large on the hands.
Moving the hands backward during the catch makes the same ball easier to handle during the stop because the stopping time increases.
The ball's momentum still changes, but the change is spread over a longer time instead of one sudden jolt through the hands.
Impulse is force multiplied by time, and it equals the change in momentum during a push, collision, or stop between objects.
Gloves, airbags, mats, and crumple zones all use the same principle: stretch the stop so the force becomes smaller at impact.

boards.title: The Reaction Recipe
layers: Iron left outside in rain changes over time, and the shiny metal begins to rust on the surface as oxygen reacts.
The iron has not vanished. Its atoms have joined with oxygen from the air to make a new substance on the metal.
A chemical reaction rearranges atoms. It does not make the atoms disappear from the material world; it changes their connections.
The starting substances are reactants. The substances formed afterward are products of the same rearrangement of atoms across the reaction.
Chemistry keeps count of which atoms were present before and where those atoms ended up after the reaction in the products.

boards.title: Balancing the Atoms
layers: If a reaction begins with six carbon atoms, the products must still contain six carbon atoms afterward on the product side.
The atoms may be rearranged into new molecules, but the count of each element is preserved through the reaction rather than destroyed.
Balancing a chemical equation is atom bookkeeping: count before, count after, then adjust whole molecules until the counts match on both sides.
The number of molecules can change, but the formula inside a molecule is not edited during balancing because that changes the substance.
The equation is balanced when every element has the same count on both sides of the reaction arrow after adjustment.

boards.title: Heat in a Reaction
layers: Strike a match, and the reaction gives off heat and light almost immediately from the flame as substances change inside the match head.
The atoms are rearranging, and energy is being transferred to the surroundings as heat and light during the reaction in the flame.
Some reactions release energy and warm the surroundings. Other reactions absorb energy and lower the nearby temperature during the process.
Chemical bonds belong in the energy account, because breaking and making bonds changes stored energy in the reacting substances inside molecules.
Chemistry tracks atoms, but it also tracks the energy moving with those atoms during a reaction as bonds change and products form.

boards.title: Acids Give Protons
layers: Lemon juice tastes sharp because its molecules behave as acids when they dissolve and interact with water in the mouth.
A first model of an acid is a substance that can give away hydrogen ions when dissolved in water during reactions.
A hydrogen ion is basically a proton, so acids are often described as proton donors in many reactions in solution.
That picture will need refining later, but it already explains many common acid reactions that happen in water as proton transfers.
A tiny charged particle moving from one molecule to another can change the behaviour of a whole solution by shifting charge.

boards.title: The Address Problem
layers: Computer memory can be pictured as a long hallway of numbered lockers, each holding a small piece of information at an address.
To read the right locker, the computer needs an address, not a vague description of where the value might be.
Memory works like this: stored values live in numbered places the machine can point to directly instead of searching by description.
A program can ask for the value at an address, change it, or use the stored value in a calculation.
Before software does anything large, the machine is already doing a lot of careful pointing between addresses and values while it runs.

boards.title: The Stack
layers: Stack plates in a cupboard, and the last plate placed on top is the first one removed from the pile.
Computers use a similar idea when a program enters a function and later returns from it in the right order.
The stack remembers short-lived information: where to return, local values, and unfinished work for the current function call inside the program.
When the function finishes, its stack space is cleared, like removing the top plate from the pile above it during return.
The stack lets a program enter a smaller job, finish it, and return to the larger job without losing its place.

boards.title: Packets
layers: A long message sent across a network usually does not travel as one huge lump from start to finish across machines.
It is broken into smaller packets, each carrying data and information about where it should go across the network toward its destination.
Packets can travel through different routes, arrive out of order, and still be reassembled into the message at the end.
This makes networks flexible, because one broken path does not have to stop the whole message from moving through another route.
The internet is less like one pipe and more like a postal system for small numbered pieces moving between machines.

boards.title: DNS
layers: A website name is easy for humans to remember, but machines need a more exact destination on the network before sending data.
The network cannot send a request to "the site I meant." It needs an address that points to a machine.
DNS is the lookup system that turns a name like example.com into an address machines can use for routing.
Without DNS, web addresses would work more like memorised phone numbers than human-readable names for every site on the network.
DNS is one of the translation layers that hides the addressing system underneath ordinary website names used by machines during lookup.

boards.title: Keeping Count
layers: A balanced chemical equation, a momentum collision, and a computer memory address look unrelated at first because their objects differ.
All three depend on keeping track of what goes where during a change from one state to another without losing count.
Chemistry tracks atoms, physics tracks quantities like energy and momentum, and computing tracks values in memory as systems change over time.
Mathematics supplies the language for that tracking: numbers, rules, graphs, and equations for comparing quantities across different systems and changes.
The subjects separate on the surface, then meet again when the counting becomes serious across different problems, materials, and motions.

boards.title: Rate
layers: Slope on a graph, velocity, reaction rate, and network speed share the same mathematical structure.
Each compares a change in one quantity with a change in another quantity over the same interval.
Position per time gives velocity. Product formed per time gives reaction rate. Data per time gives bandwidth.
Mathematics gives the reusable pattern, and each science attaches that pattern to its own kind of change.
Rate is one place where different subjects use the same structure under different names.

boards.title: Following Energy
layers: A falling ball, a burning match, and a glowing screen all ask the same question about energy during change across different processes.
The central question is where the energy came from, where it went, and what changed while it moved between forms.
In physics, energy changes between height, motion, heat, sound, and other forms during events such as falls, collisions, and heating.
In chemistry, energy is tied to bonds breaking and forming during reactions between atoms in molecules and materials as products form.
In computing, electrical energy is spent moving charge through circuits and switching transistors on and off inside processors many times.

boards.title: Reaction Rate
layers: Drop an effervescent tablet into cold water, and the bubbles appear slowly at first around the tablet as gas forms.
Drop the same kind of tablet into warm water, and the fizz usually becomes faster almost immediately as particle motion increases.
The reaction is similar, but the speed of the reaction has changed because the conditions changed inside the water around the tablet.
A reaction rate measures how quickly reactants turn into products during a chemical change over a measured time in a system.
Chemistry often asks what will form, and also how fast that product will form under the chosen conditions during a reaction.

boards.title: A limit studies approach
layers: A function gives outputs from inputs, but calculus often asks what happens as the input moves toward a chosen value.
A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input gets closer and closer to a point from nearby inputs.
The point being approached does not need to be reached for the nearby behavior of the function to become clear.
This is the first bridge from functions to calculus: studying motion toward a value rather than only evaluating at the value.
Limits make it possible to talk precisely about trends, gaps, curves, rates, and change near a point on a function.

boards.title: Nearby values can reveal a pattern

tags.concept: Nearby values can reveal a pattern
tags.subject: maths

layers: A limit is usually found by looking at function values close to the input being studied, rather than only at the input itself.
If values from the left and right both move toward the same output, the function has a limit there at that point.
The actual value of the function at the point may agree with the limit, differ from it, or be undefined.
This separates local behavior from direct substitution, which is why limits are useful when formulas have gaps or undefined points.
The important question is not only what the function equals, but what the function is approaching nearby from both sides.

boards.title: Left and right must agree
layers: A two-sided limit exists only when the function approaches the same value from both directions around the input being studied.
The left-hand limit studies inputs smaller than the point, while the right-hand limit studies inputs larger than the point being approached.
If both sides approach the same output, the two-sided limit exists and equals that shared value at the point itself.
If the left and right sides approach different values, the function has no single limit at that point on the graph.
This matters because calculus depends on stable local behavior, not on two directions giving conflicting answers near the same input.

boards.title: Holes and jumps behave differently
layers: A hole occurs when the nearby values approach one output, but the function is missing or defined differently at the point.
In that case, the limit can still exist because the surrounding behavior points toward one clear value from both sides.
A jump occurs when the function approaches one value from the left and another value from the right at the same input.
A jump has no two-sided limit at the jump point because the two approaches disagree with each other there completely.
Limits therefore distinguish between removable breaks, where the nearby pattern is stable, and jumps, where the pattern splits into two sides.

boards.title: Limits handle impossible substitution
layers: Some formulas cannot be evaluated directly at a point because substitution creates an expression such as division by zero in the formula.
A limit asks whether the formula still approaches a stable value as the input gets close to that point from nearby values.
Algebra can sometimes simplify the expression and reveal the value that the nearby points were approaching all along in the pattern.
This does not pretend the forbidden input is allowed. It studies the behavior around the forbidden input instead, using nearby values.
That distinction is essential for calculus, where meaningful patterns often appear at points that direct substitution cannot handle cleanly by itself.

boards.title: Limits can describe infinity
layers: Some limits study what happens as the input grows without bound instead of approaching a fixed number on the number line.
A function may approach a horizontal level as x becomes very large or very negative over the long run in the graph.
That horizontal level is called a horizontal asymptote when the graph gets closer to it over the long run without necessarily touching it.
Other functions grow without bound, meaning their outputs become larger and larger instead of settling near a finite value at all.
Limits at infinity describe long-term behavior, which is useful in graphs, models, sequences, and rates of decay over time and change.

boards.title: Continuity means no break in the limit

tags.concept: Continuity means no break in the limit
tags.subject: maths

layers: A function is continuous at a point when its value and its limit at that point agree exactly with each other.
That means the function is defined there, the nearby values approach a limit, and the limit equals the function value.
On a graph, continuity means the curve passes through the point without a hole, jump, or break in its path.
Continuity is not only a visual idea. It is a statement about the agreement between value and approach at a point.
This prepares the ground for differentiation, because derivatives require stable behavior near the point being studied on the curve itself.

boards.title: Limits measure shrinking change
layers: The second bridge to differentiation begins when a limit is used to study change over smaller and smaller intervals around a point.
A secant slope measures average change between two points on a curve by comparing vertical change with horizontal change between them.
As the two points move closer together, the secant slope may approach one stable value at the chosen point on the curve.
That limiting value is the slope of the tangent line at the point, if the limit exists there for the curve.
Differentiation begins here: the derivative is a limit of average rates of change as the interval shrinks to zero at the point.

boards.title: Derivatives describe motion
layers: Derivatives are not only geometric slopes. They also describe rates of change in quantities that vary over time or space.
Velocity is the derivative of position because it measures how quickly position changes with respect to time or another time unit.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity because it measures how quickly velocity itself changes over time during motion along a path.
Similar rate ideas appear in temperature change, medicine concentration, current flow, population change, and energy transfer in physical systems over time.
In each case, differentiation gives a precise language for how fast one quantity is changing relative to another quantity in context.

boards.title: Derivatives locate turning points
layers: A derivative can show where a function is increasing, decreasing, or flattening out across a chosen interval on the graph itself.
When the derivative is positive, the function is rising. When the derivative is negative, the function is falling on that interval.
Points where the derivative equals zero can mark local maxima, local minima, or flat points that are neither in context.
Optimization uses this information to find best values, such as maximum height, minimum cost, or most efficient design for a problem.
This makes differentiation a tool for studying change, motion, and decisions, not only for finding slopes on graphs alone in isolation.
